## Which databases do Prisma ORM and Kysely support?

Kysely's dialects next to the two Prisma ORM lines. Prisma ORM 7 is the generally available release, and it supports every database here except PGlite. No means no support.

| Database | Kysely | Prisma ORM 8 | Prisma ORM 7 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | Built-in | Release candidate | Supported | 
| MySQL | Built-in | ORM 7 only | Supported | 
| MariaDB | Community dialect | ORM 7 only | Supported | 
| Microsoft SQL Server | Built-in | ORM 7 only | Supported | 
| SQLite | Built-in | Experimental | Supported | 
| CockroachDB | No | ORM 7 only | Supported | 
| MongoDB | No | Early access | Supported | 
| PGlite | Built-in | No | No | 

MariaDB on Kysely is the community [kysely-mariadb](https://github.com/awaludinar/kysely-mariadb) dialect. Sources: [Kysely dialects](https://kysely.dev/docs/dialects), [Prisma ORM 8 supported databases](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/supported-databases), and [Prisma ORM 7 supported databases](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/reference/supported-databases), October 2026.

payload.content:
## When is Prisma ORM the wrong choice?

- You want a SQL query builder and no contract file. Kysely takes a TypeScript `Database` interface, a dialect, and that dialect's driver.
- You need MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, or CockroachDB from the current Prisma ORM 8 packages. Those databases are not in ORM 8 yet. [Prisma ORM 7](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7) still supports them, and Kysely has built-in dialects for MySQL, SQL Server, and SQLite. payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: How does each task look in Kysely and Prisma ORM?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Kysely: contract file or SQL query builder? > How does each task look in Kysely and Prisma ORM?
payload.content:
## How does each task look in Kysely and Prisma ORM?

What each step of the usual workflow looks like on each side, for a team moving in either direction.

| Task | Kysely | Prisma ORM | 
|---|---|---|
| Define tables | A TypeScript `Database` interface, with one property per table. | Models in `contract.prisma`. | 
| Generate types | Nothing to generate if you write the interface by hand. Community generators such as `kysely-codegen` write it for you. | `contract emit` writes the types from the contract. | 
| Read an existing database | `kysely-codegen` connects to PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, or SQL Server and writes the `Database` interface. | Inspects a live database and writes a starter `contract.prisma`. | 
| Write a migration | `up` and `down` functions you write with `db.schema`. `kysely migrate make` from `kysely-ctl` creates the file. | `migration plan` writes `migration.ts` from the contract. | 
| Preview query SQL | `.compile()` on a query returns its SQL and parameters without running it. | `.build()` on the SQL query builder returns the query without running it. | 
| Preview migration SQL | You read the SQL you wrote in the `up` function. There is no separate preview command. | A CLI preview prints a migration's operations and statement preview, without connecting to the database. | 
| Run migrations | `Migrator` from `kysely/migration`, with `migrateToLatest()`. `kysely-ctl` wraps it as `kysely migrate latest`. | `db migrate` applies the pending migrations on disk. |

payload.content:
## How do I switch from Prisma ORM to Kysely?

1. Keep the database and the connection string.
2. Add a TypeScript `Database` interface that matches the tables. A community generator can emit those types from a Prisma schema. Prisma documents it on the [Prisma ORM 7 generators](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/prisma-schema/overview/generators) page. It is not part of Prisma ORM.
3. Create one Kysely instance with the dialect that matches the database, plus that dialect's driver. On PostgreSQL that is `PostgresDialect` and `pg`. On Prisma Postgres, follow the [Kysely quickstart](https://www.prisma.io/docs/prisma-postgres/quickstart/kysely). Prisma ORM is optional there.

## Frequently asked questions

Yes. Kysely ships a migrator that runs the `up` and `down` functions you write by hand, so many teams add a separate tool to generate them. Prisma writes the migration for you from your schema. In Prisma 7, `prisma migrate dev` compares your schema with the database, writes a plain SQL file you can edit, and applies it, while `prisma migrate deploy` applies migrations in production. Prisma 8 (release candidate) keeps the idea with new commands: `prisma migration plan` writes a TypeScript migration you can review, and `prisma db migrate` applies it. To try it, [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/postgres) has a free plan with 50 databases, 2 GB and 200k operations a month, no card needed.

Both give you typed MongoDB access in TypeScript, from opposite ends. [Prisma ORM](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm) starts from a contract file: you describe your collections once, and typed queries, aggregations, and migrations follow from it. [Mongoose](https://mongoosejs.com) starts from a Schema in application code: you compile it with `mongoose.model` and query with `find()` and `populate()`.

[Get started with Prisma ORM](https://www.prisma.io/docs/prisma-orm/quickstart/postgresql) [Create an instant database](https://create-db.prisma.io/web)

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: When should I choose Mongoose or Prisma ORM?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > When should I choose Mongoose or Prisma ORM?
payload.content:
## When should I choose Mongoose or Prisma ORM?

| Mongoose | Prisma ORM | 
|---|---|
| You want the schema next to the model in application code, compiled with `mongoose.model`. | You want models in a contract file, `contract.prisma` — a contract is the file that describes your collections or tables. | 
| You want `populate()` to replace a stored id with a document from another collection. | You want `contract emit` to write the query types. Prisma ORM 8 does not use the `@prisma/client` package. That package is Prisma ORM 7. | 
| You want pre and post hooks on documents, queries, aggregates, and models. | You want a typed aggregation pipeline, polymorphic collections from `@@discriminator`, and `migration plan` to write `migration.ts` for indexes and JSON Schema validators. `db migrate` runs `ops.json`. | 
| The database is MongoDB, and `find()` should take MongoDB query operators. | You also ship on PostgreSQL, where the release candidate includes the ORM client, a SQL query builder, and relation filters. | 

MongoDB's May 2026 post [Prisma Next: The TypeScript ODM You Always Wanted](https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/technical/prisma-next-typescript-odm-you-always-wanted) is their write-up of this work: typed documents, a typed aggregation pipeline, and migrations for indexes instead of a deploy script. On prisma.io the same library is Prisma ORM 8's MongoDB early access, not a separate product named Prisma Next.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: How do Prisma ORM and Mongoose compare feature by feature?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > How do Prisma ORM and Mongoose compare feature by feature?
payload.content:
## How do Prisma ORM and Mongoose compare feature by feature?

Mongoose models MongoDB documents in application code. Prisma ORM is a contract-based ORM with a typed pipeline, polymorphic collections, and MongoDB migrations for indexes and validators. On MongoDB the PostgreSQL APIs (SQL query builder, relation filters) are absent. Columns are in alphabetical order.

| Feature | Mongoose | Prisma ORM | 
|---|---|---|
| Library price | Free. MIT license. | Free. Apache License 2.0. | 
| Release status | Version 9.11.2 on npm. Mongoose 9.0.0 shipped on 21 November 2025. The getting started guide is this 9.x line. | Prisma ORM 8 is a release candidate, and it is what `npm install prisma` gives you. The final release is still to come. PostgreSQL is the release-candidate database. MongoDB is early access. | 
| Data model | A Schema and a Model in application code. `mongoose.model` compiles the schema. | A contract file, `contract.prisma`. On MongoDB you write that file yourself: `contract infer` does not read a MongoDB database. `contract emit` writes the types. There is no `@prisma/client` package. | 
| Queries | `Model.find()` and the other query helpers, with MongoDB query operators. | An ORM client, `db.orm.<collection>`, addressed by the storage name (`db.orm.posts`, not `db.orm.Post`). A pipeline builder for aggregation, and raw commands for anything the two APIs do not cover. | 
| Embedded documents | Nested schemas and subdocuments on the parent document. | A `type` block in the contract, used as a field. Embedded values have no `_id` and no collection of their own. |

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: How do Prisma ORM and Mongoose compare feature by feature?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > How do Prisma ORM and Mongoose compare feature by feature?
payload.content:
| Embedded documents | Nested schemas and subdocuments on the parent document. | A `type` block in the contract, used as a field. Embedded values have no `_id` and no collection of their own. | 
| Polymorphic collections | `Model.discriminator()` stores variants in one collection. Variant fields are optional or split across schemas you keep in application code. | `@@discriminator` on the base model and `@@base` on each variant. `db.orm.posts.variant('article')` narrows the TypeScript type. Query all posts and you get the union. | 
| Aggregation | `Model.aggregate()` takes a pipeline array. Stages are not type-checked. | The pipeline builder at `db.query` types field names and each stage's output. Raw commands cover stages the builder does not. | 
| Related documents | `populate()` loads related documents in a separate query. `match` filters which of those documents are attached, and the parent stays in the result. `populate()` cannot filter parents by a field on the related document. | On MongoDB, `include()` loads a reference declared with `@relation`, and it takes the relation name only. An array of ids stored on the parent has no `include()` equivalent yet; the migrate guide uses `lookup` in the pipeline builder. Relation filters are not available on MongoDB. On PostgreSQL, `where` can use `some`, `none`, and `every`. | 
| Middleware | pre and post hooks. Four kinds: document, model, aggregate, and query middleware. | Middleware runs on MongoDB, except `beforeCompile`, which exists on PostgreSQL. The cache middleware runs on both databases. |

payload.content:
| Middleware | pre and post hooks. Four kinds: document, model, aggregate, and query middleware. | Middleware runs on MongoDB, except `beforeCompile`, which exists on PostgreSQL. The cache middleware runs on both databases. | 
| Migrations | The getting started guide has no migration command. | `migration plan` writes `migration.ts` from the contract. Planning does not connect to a database. `db migrate` runs `ops.json`. On MongoDB that file can create collections, indexes, and JSON Schema validators, and it can run a `dataTransform`. | 
| Databases | MongoDB. The README describes Mongoose as a MongoDB object modeling tool. | PostgreSQL is a release candidate. MongoDB is early access. SQLite is experimental. MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, and CockroachDB stay on Prisma ORM 7. See [database support](https://www.prisma.io#databases). | 
| Hosted database | None. Mongoose is a library. You bring MongoDB. | [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres) is a separate product. Any Postgres client works with it, so Prisma ORM is optional. Mongoose connects to MongoDB, so it does not connect to Prisma Postgres. [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) is separate app hosting. |

payload.section: Which databases do Prisma ORM and Mongoose support?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > Which databases do Prisma ORM and Mongoose support?
payload.content:
## Which databases do Prisma ORM and Mongoose support?

Mongoose's MongoDB support next to the two Prisma ORM lines. Prisma ORM 7 is the generally available release. No means no support. The [MongoDB product page](https://www.prisma.io/mongodb) describes Prisma's schema and type-safe client for MongoDB, including embedded documents and references. Its query samples use Prisma Client's `findMany` API from earlier Prisma ORM lines. Prisma ORM 8 queries go through `db.orm.<collection>`.

| Database | Mongoose | Prisma ORM 8 | Prisma ORM 7 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| MongoDB | Supported | Early access | Use 6.19 | 
| PostgreSQL | No | Release candidate | Supported | 
| MySQL | No | ORM 7 only | Supported | 
| MariaDB | No | ORM 7 only | Supported | 
| Microsoft SQL Server | No | ORM 7 only | Supported | 
| SQLite | No | Experimental | Supported | 
| CockroachDB | No | ORM 7 only | Supported | 

MongoDB on Prisma ORM 7 is listed as supported on the ORM 7 databases page. The ORM 7 [migrate-from-Mongoose guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/v7/switch-to-prisma-orm/from-mongoose) says Prisma ORM 7 has no MongoDB connector yet, and to stay on 6.19 until it ships. This table follows that guide for MongoDB. Sources: [Mongoose README](https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/blob/master/README.md), [Prisma ORM 8 supported databases](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/supported-databases), and [Prisma ORM 7 supported databases](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/reference/supported-databases), October 2026.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > A typed aggregation pipeline
payload.content:
## A typed aggregation pipeline

Mongoose's `aggregate()` takes a pipeline array. Prisma ORM 8's MongoDB library has a pipeline builder that types field names and the shape after each stage, then you drop to raw commands when the builder does not cover a stage. [MongoDB without compromise](https://www.prisma.io/blog/mongodb-without-compromise) is the Prisma write-up of that stack, checked against the [pipeline builder](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/reference/pipeline-builder).

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > Polymorphic collections from the contract
payload.content:
## Polymorphic collections from the contract

`@@discriminator` and `@@base` declare variants in one collection, and `.variant('article')` narrows the TypeScript union. Mongoose has [`discriminator()`](https://mongoosejs.com/docs/discriminators.html) too; the Prisma side generates the unions from the contract. MongoDB's [Prisma Next post](https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/technical/prisma-next-typescript-odm-you-always-wanted) says their Driver team named this as the top missing feature in earlier Prisma ORM. The [MongoDB data modeling](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/data-modeling/mongodb) docs are the current syntax.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > Migrations for indexes and validators
payload.content:
## Migrations for indexes and validators

`migration plan` writes `migration.ts` without connecting to the database. On MongoDB, `db migrate` can create collections, indexes, and JSON Schema validators, and it can run a `dataTransform`. The April 2026 [MongoDB without compromise](https://www.prisma.io/blog/mongodb-without-compromise) post said data migrations were still coming; the [migration API](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/reference/migration-api) now documents `dataTransform` on MongoDB.

payload.section: The same ORM client on PostgreSQL
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > The same ORM client on PostgreSQL
payload.content:
## The same ORM client on PostgreSQL

Mongoose speaks MongoDB. Prisma ORM 8's PostgreSQL library is a release candidate: the ORM client, a SQL query builder, and relation filters (`some`, `none`, `every`) that the MongoDB client does not have.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: When is Prisma ORM the wrong choice?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > When is Prisma ORM the wrong choice?
payload.content:
## When is Prisma ORM the wrong choice?

- You want document and query middleware, and `populate()` on arrays of stored ids, from a MongoDB library that is already a stable release. Prisma ORM 8's MongoDB library is early access. An array of ids has no `include()` equivalent yet. See [migrate from Mongoose](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/switch-to-prisma-orm/from-mongoose).
- You want multi-document transactions on MongoDB. `db.transaction()` is absent on the MongoDB client. Multi-document writes go through the MongoDB driver. See [supported databases](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/supported-databases).
- You need MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, or CockroachDB from the current Prisma ORM 8 packages. Those databases are absent from ORM 8. [Prisma ORM 7](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7) still supports them. Mongoose speaks MongoDB. See [supported databases](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/supported-databases).

payload.section: How does each task look in Mongoose and Prisma ORM?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > How does each task look in Mongoose and Prisma ORM?
payload.content:
## How does each task look in Mongoose and Prisma ORM?

What each step of the usual workflow looks like on each side, for a team moving in either direction.

| Task | Mongoose | Prisma ORM | 
|---|---|---|
| Define collections | A `Schema` compiled with `mongoose.model`. | Models in `contract.prisma`, with `@@map` for the collection name. | 
| Generate types | TypeScript types you write, or types inferred from the schema in application code. | `contract emit` writes the types from the contract. | 
| Read an existing database | The schemas in the app are the source of truth. MongoDB has no schema to infer. | `contract infer` does not read MongoDB. You write `contract.prisma` from the Mongoose schemas. | 
| Write a migration | The getting started guide has no migration command. You change documents in code. | `migration plan` writes `migration.ts`. On MongoDB that can include `createIndex`, `setValidation`, and `dataTransform`. | 
| Run an aggregation | `Model.aggregate([...])` with untyped pipeline stages. | `db.query.from('<collection>')`, then `runtime.query(...)` or `runtime.execute(...)`. | 
| Query a polymorphic collection | `Model.discriminator()` and query the discriminator model. | `@@discriminator` / `@@base` in the contract, then `.variant('article')` on the base collection. | 
| Load a related document | `populate()` on a stored id. `match` can narrow which related documents come back. | `include()` on a single `@relation`. An array of ids has no `include()` equivalent yet; use `lookup` in the pipeline builder. | 
| Run middleware | pre and post hooks on documents, queries, aggregates, and models. | Middleware on MongoDB, except `beforeCompile`. The cache middleware runs on MongoDB. |

| Run middleware | pre and post hooks on documents, queries, aggregates, and models. | Middleware on MongoDB, except `beforeCompile`. The cache middleware runs on MongoDB. | 
| Apply schema changes | You update documents yourself. There is no Mongoose migrate command in the guide. | `db migrate` applies the pending migrations on disk. |

The [migrate-from-Mongoose guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/switch-to-prisma-orm/from-mongoose) adds Prisma ORM beside the collections you already have. `orm init --target mongodb` writes the Prisma files. `contract infer` does not read a MongoDB database, so you write `contract.prisma` from the Mongoose schemas, then `contract emit` writes the types. payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma ORM vs Mongoose: contract file or schema in application code? > How do I switch from Prisma ORM to Mongoose?
payload.content:
## How do I switch from Prisma ORM to Mongoose?

1. Keep the MongoDB database and the connection string.
2. Define a `Schema` and compile it with `mongoose.model` for each collection. The [getting started guide](https://mongoosejs.com/docs/) is that path.
3. Use `populate()` on stored ids. Prisma ORM's `include()` on MongoDB covers a single `@relation`; an array of ids uses `lookup` in the pipeline builder.

## Prisma Postgres vs Neon: TypeScript app hosting or Neon backend primitives?

Pick [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres) when you want managed PostgreSQL with [Prisma ORM](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm) optional, and [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) hosting the TypeScript app as HTTP services in the same Prisma project. Pick [Neon](https://neon.com/docs/get-started/backend-overview) when you want Postgres plus Functions, Managed Better Auth, Object Storage, and AI Gateway, with the UI on a host such as Vercel or Netlify.

[Get started with Prisma Postgres](https://console.prisma.io) [Create an instant database](https://create-db.prisma.io/web)

By [Martin Janse van Rensburg](https://www.prisma.io/blog/author/martin-janse-van-rensburg) · Updated  · 10 min read[X](https://x.com/vanrensbird)[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/martjvr/)[GitHub](https://github.com/vanrensbird)

payload.section: When should I choose Neon or Prisma Postgres?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma Postgres vs Neon: TypeScript app hosting or Neon backend primitives? > When should I choose Neon or Prisma Postgres?
payload.content:
## When should I choose Neon or Prisma Postgres?

| Neon | Prisma Postgres | 
|---|---|
| You want Neon Functions, Managed Better Auth, Object Storage, and AI Gateway next to Postgres, declared in one `neon.ts`. | You want [Prisma ORM](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm) available on the same platform as the database. Prisma ORM is optional; any Postgres client works. | 
| You want the UI on a host such as Vercel or Netlify, with Neon running the backend next to the database. | You want [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) to host the TypeScript app as HTTP services next to [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres). | 
| You want copy-on-write database branches that include parent data, and instant restore within the plan's history window. | You want a [preview branch](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/branching) that can own its app services and database. | 
| You want database compute billed in CU-hours that go to $0 while scale-to-zero has suspended the compute. | You prefer operation-based database pricing with spend limits on paid plans. | 

Want the whole app, frontend included, hosted next to the database? See [Neon alternatives with app hosting and Postgres in one place (2026)](https://www.prisma.io/blog/neon-vs-prisma-postgres-app-hosting-in-one-place) and, for more hosts, [App hosting platforms with managed Postgres compared (2026)](https://www.prisma.io/blog/app-hosting-platforms-with-managed-postgres-2026).

payload.section: How do Neon and Prisma Postgres compare?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma Postgres vs Neon: TypeScript app hosting or Neon backend primitives? > How do Neon and Prisma Postgres compare?
payload.content:
## How do Neon and Prisma Postgres compare?

Neon and Prisma Postgres are both managed PostgreSQL. Neon adds backend primitives next to the database and keeps full-app hosting on a separate platform. Prisma Postgres sits next to an optional ORM and Prisma Compute. Columns are in alphabetical order.

| Feature | Neon | Prisma Postgres | 
|---|---|---|
| Database | Managed PostgreSQL (Lakebase Postgres) with autoscaling, connection pooling, and scale-to-zero. Works with any language, framework, or ORM that supports Postgres. | [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres) is managed PostgreSQL that autoscales, with no instance to size or upgrade. Prisma Postgres has no cold starts. Any Postgres client works with it, so Prisma ORM is optional. | 
| ORM on the same platform | No first-party ORM. Teams pick an external ORM or SQL client, such as Drizzle or Prisma ORM pointed at Neon. | [Prisma ORM](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm) is a first-party type-safe ORM on the same platform. It is optional. | 
| App hosting | Neon Functions run backend logic next to the database. Neon recommends hosting the UI on a separate platform such as Vercel or Netlify. | [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) hosts the TypeScript app as HTTP services. It is separate from Prisma Postgres. Compute has no built-in cron scheduler today; native cron is planned for early 2027. WebSocket servers are not supported today; support is planned for early 2027. |

| Branches and previews | A Neon branch is a copy-on-write clone of Postgres. Object Storage, Functions, Auth, and AI Gateway can branch with the data. The Neon-managed Vercel integration can create a database branch per preview deployment. | A Prisma [preview branch](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/branching) can own its Compute services and databases. Production data is not copied into that database. |

payload.content:
## When is Prisma Postgres the wrong choice?

- You want Neon Functions, Managed Better Auth, Object Storage, or AI Gateway as first-party primitives next to Postgres. Prisma Postgres does not include those. See [How a Neon backend fits together](https://neon.com/docs/get-started/backend-overview).

On paid plans, Prisma Postgres restores daily backups, taken only on days the database has activity, in place or into a new database, and point-in-time recovery is coming in November 2026. Neon documents instant restore on paid plans at [Neon pricing](https://neon.com/pricing).
- You want database compute that bills $0 while the instance is suspended, rather than operation-based pricing. Neon CU-hours stop while scale-to-zero has suspended compute; storage still bills.

payload.content:
## How do I switch from Neon to Prisma Postgres?

1. Create an empty Prisma Postgres database. Prisma ORM is optional. The [migrate from Neon](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/switch-to-prisma-postgres/from-neon) guide uses `pg_dump` and `pg_restore` over the direct connection.
2. Dump the selected Neon branch and database with a direct (non-pooler) connection string, then restore into Prisma Postgres. The dump copies PostgreSQL schemas and data. It does not reproduce Neon branch history, Functions, Auth, Object Storage, or other Neon backend services.
3. Point the app at the Prisma Postgres connection string. Host the HTTP app on Prisma Compute, or keep the frontend host you already use.

payload.content:

1. Create a Neon project and dump Prisma Postgres with `pg_dump` over the direct connection, then restore into Neon. Both sides are PostgreSQL.
2. Point the app at the Neon `DATABASE_URL`. Keep using SQL or an ORM; Neon has no first-party ORM.
3. Publish the UI with a provider such as Vercel or Netlify, as the [full-backend guide](https://neon.com/docs/get-started/full-backend-quickstart) describes. Add Functions, Auth, Object Storage, or AI Gateway in `neon.ts` if you need those primitives. Prisma Postgres stays in place until you stop using it.

| You want the UI on a host such as Vercel, with Supabase running the backend next to the database. | You want [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) to host the TypeScript app as HTTP services next to [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres). | 
| You want isolated Supabase preview environments for the backend, with frontend previews on an external host. | You want a [preview branch](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/branching) that can own its app services and database. |

## How do Supabase and Prisma Postgres compare?

Supabase and Prisma Postgres are both managed PostgreSQL. Supabase adds Auth, Storage, Realtime, APIs, and Edge Functions around the database. Prisma Postgres sits next to an optional ORM and Prisma Compute. Columns are Supabase, then Prisma Postgres.

| Feature | Supabase | Prisma Postgres | 
|---|---|---|
| Database | Managed PostgreSQL. A project can be used as a standalone Postgres database with any Postgres client. Auth, Storage, Realtime, and Edge Functions are included and optional. | [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres) is managed PostgreSQL that autoscales, with no instance to size or upgrade. Any Postgres client works with it, so Prisma ORM is optional. | 
| ORM on the same platform | Auto-generated APIs and client libraries. Teams pick an external ORM or SQL client, such as Prisma ORM pointed at Supabase. | [Prisma ORM](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm) is a first-party type-safe ORM on the same platform. It is optional. | 
| App hosting | Edge Functions run server-side logic next to the database. Full app and frontend hosting remains on a separate platform. | [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) hosts the TypeScript app as HTTP services. It is separate from Prisma Postgres. Compute has no built-in cron scheduler. WebSocket servers are not supported. |

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma Postgres vs Supabase: what's the difference and which should I pick? > When is Prisma Postgres the wrong choice?
payload.content:
## When is Prisma Postgres the wrong choice?

- You want Auth, Storage, Realtime, auto-generated APIs, or Edge Functions as first-party services next to Postgres. Prisma Postgres does not include those. See [Supabase pricing](https://supabase.com/pricing).
- You want the frontend on a host such as Vercel, with Supabase isolating Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, and the database on a preview branch. A Prisma preview branch can own Compute services and databases; it does not include those Supabase backend products. See [Supabase branching](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/deployment/branching).
- You need point-in-time recovery today. Prisma Postgres has no point-in-time recovery yet (it is coming in November 2026). Paid plans include daily backups. Supabase sells PITR as a $100 per month add-on per 7 days of retention on [Supabase pricing](https://supabase.com/pricing).
- You want database compute billed by the hour with a $25 Pro base, and you are fine that the Spend Cap excludes compute. Prisma Postgres bills operations and storage instead.

payload.section: How do I switch from Supabase to Prisma Postgres?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma Postgres vs Supabase: what's the difference and which should I pick? > How do I switch from Supabase to Prisma Postgres?
payload.content:
## How do I switch from Supabase to Prisma Postgres?

1. Create an empty Prisma Postgres database. Prisma ORM is optional. The [migrate from Supabase](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/switch-to-prisma-postgres/from-supabase) guide uses `pg_dump` and `pg_restore` over the direct connection.
2. Dump the PostgreSQL application data you own, then restore into Prisma Postgres. The dump copies schemas and data. It does not migrate Auth users, Storage objects, Realtime configuration, or Edge Functions.
3. Point the app at the Prisma Postgres connection string. Host the HTTP app on Prisma Compute, or keep the frontend host you already use. Replace any Auth, Storage, or Realtime calls before you switch production traffic.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma Postgres vs Supabase: what's the difference and which should I pick? > How do I switch from Prisma Postgres to Supabase?
payload.content:
## How do I switch from Prisma Postgres to Supabase?

1. Create a Supabase project and dump Prisma Postgres with `pg_dump` over the direct connection, then restore into Supabase. Both sides are PostgreSQL.
2. Point the app at the Supabase connection string. Keep using SQL or an ORM; Supabase has no first-party ORM.
3. Publish the UI on a separate host. Add Auth, Storage, Realtime, or Edge Functions if you need those products. Prisma Postgres stays in place until you stop using it.

## When should I choose Vercel + Neon + Drizzle or Prisma?

| Vercel + Neon + Drizzle | Prisma |

Start with [Prisma ORM](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm) and add [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres) and [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) as your needs grow. |

payload.content:
## How do Vercel + Neon + Drizzle and Prisma compare?

Both cover a TypeScript backend: an ORM, managed Postgres, and a place to run the app. Vercel, Neon, and Drizzle are three products you wire together. Prisma ORM, Prisma Postgres, and Prisma Compute sit in one platform.

| Backend need | Vercel + Neon + Drizzle | Prisma | 
|---|---|---|
| Core setup | Choose and wire Drizzle, Neon, and Vercel across three providers. | [Prisma ORM](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm), [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres), and [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) in one platform. | 
| Data model | Drizzle schema in your app code, connected to a Neon database. | One Prisma schema that the ORM, migrations, and the CLI all read. | 
| Environments | A Neon branch per Vercel preview deployment through the Neon integration for Vercel, cloned from production data. | A Prisma [preview branch](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/branching) owns its app services and its own database, which starts empty. | 
| Agent workflow | The agent moves across three vendors' tools and docs. | The agent works through the Prisma schema, CLI, and [REST API](https://www.prisma.io/docs/rest-api). | 
| Billing | Neon bills compute in CU-hours plus storage. Vercel bills a Pro seat plus usage. Drizzle is free. Neon installed from the Vercel Marketplace is billed through Vercel. | Prisma Postgres and Prisma Compute share one set of plans, billed by operations and storage, with spend limits on paid plans. |

payload.content:
## Vercel + Neon + Drizzle

This setup combines three products to cover the app, the database, and the data layer.

[Drizzle](https://orm.drizzle.team) is the data layer: a free, open-source, type-safe TypeScript ORM and query builder. It connects to a database you host somewhere else. See [how Prisma ORM compares to Drizzle](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/more/comparisons/prisma-and-drizzle).

[Neon](https://neon.com) is the database: serverless Postgres with branching and scale-to-zero, billed by compute.

[Vercel](https://vercel.com) is the host. It runs your frontend and full-stack app with serverless functions.

Each product handles its own layer. You connect them yourself, keep environments in step across providers, and watch two pricing models.

- You want to pick the tool you prefer for each layer and connect them yourself.
- You already deploy on Vercel and want Neon Postgres installed from the Vercel Marketplace.
- You prefer Drizzle's SQL-first, query-builder style.
- You want preview databases that start as copy-on-write clones of production data.

[Prisma ORM](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm) is a type-safe data layer built around a declarative Prisma schema.

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres) is managed Postgres in the same project as your services.

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) hosts TypeScript apps next to Prisma Postgres, with a preview environment per branch.

One CLI and one [REST API](https://www.prisma.io/docs/rest-api) manage all three, for developers and coding agents alike.

- You want fewer integrations to manage. The ORM, the database, and the hosting come from one platform.
- You use coding agents throughout development. They work from one Prisma schema, one CLI, and one API.
- You want each preview and staging environment to own its app services and its database.
- You want one stack from early development onward. Start with Prisma ORM and add Prisma Postgres and Prisma Compute as your needs grow.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma vs Vercel + Neon + Drizzle: two ways to build a TypeScript backend > When is Prisma the wrong choice?
payload.content:
## When is Prisma the wrong choice?

- You want to pick the tool you prefer for each layer and connect Drizzle, Neon, and Vercel yourself. Prisma puts the ORM, database, and hosting on one platform.
- You want hosting and the database managed from the Vercel dashboard. Prisma Postgres works with an app on Vercel, but it is managed from the Prisma Console.
- You want preview databases seeded with production data. A Neon branch is a copy-on-write clone of production; a Prisma preview database starts empty.
- You prefer Drizzle's SQL-first, query-builder style. Prisma ORM uses a declarative Prisma schema. See [how Prisma ORM compares to Drizzle](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/more/comparisons/prisma-and-drizzle).

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma vs Vercel + Neon + Drizzle: two ways to build a TypeScript backend > How do I switch from Vercel + Neon + Drizzle to Prisma?
payload.content:
## How do I switch from Vercel + Neon + Drizzle to Prisma?

1. Create a Prisma Postgres database. The [import from an existing database](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/import-from-existing-database) guide uses `pg_dump` and `pg_restore` over the direct connection.
2. Move the data layer with the [switch from Drizzle](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/switch-to-prisma-orm/from-drizzle) guide if you want Prisma ORM. Prisma ORM is optional; Prisma Postgres works with any Postgres client.
3. Point the app at the Prisma Postgres connection string. Host the HTTP app on Prisma Compute, or keep Vercel if that host still fits.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Prisma vs Vercel + Neon + Drizzle: two ways to build a TypeScript backend > How do I switch from Prisma to Vercel + Neon + Drizzle?
payload.content:
## How do I switch from Prisma to Vercel + Neon + Drizzle?

1. Create a Neon database and dump Prisma Postgres with `pg_dump` over the direct connection, then restore into Neon. Both sides are PostgreSQL.
2. Point the app at the Neon connection string. Keep using SQL or an ORM; Drizzle is one option, documented on [Drizzle + Neon](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/get-started/neon-new).
3. Deploy the app on Vercel. Prisma Postgres stays in place until you stop using it.

## Where should I host a TypeScript AI assistant that saves conversations in Postgres?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)is a good fit for a TypeScript team that wants the app and database deployed in one project. You can also keep a Vercel or Netlify app and connect it to Prisma Postgres. Persist messages on the server, enforce conversation ownership and decide what happens when a model response is interrupted.

A useful assistant needs to remember what the customer sees after a refresh or a return visit. Keeping an array in the server process or rendering model tokens in the browser does not give the app durable conversation history.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The host documentation linked below was checked on October 18, 2026. Prisma ORM is optional, and the database model here does not depend on a particular model API.

payload.section: [What belongs on the server and in Postgres?](https://www.prisma.io#what-belongs-on-the-server-and-in-postgres)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host a TypeScript AI assistant that saves conversations in Postgres? > [What belongs on the server and in Postgres?](https://www.prisma.io#what-belongs-on-the-server-and-in-postgres)
payload.content:
## [What belongs on the server and in Postgres?](https://www.prisma.io#what-belongs-on-the-server-and-in-postgres)

For chat between users, use the [realtime chat database guide](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/realtime-chat-database) to compare durable messages, room permissions, presence and delivery after a reconnect.

The server authenticates the user, checks conversation access, calls the model provider and writes messages. Keep the model API key and database credentials in server-side configuration. The browser should call an application endpoint rather than connect with a database password.

Store conversations with an owner or account identifier. Store messages with a conversation reference, role, content and processing state. A request identifier helps the server recognize a retried send instead of creating another copy of the user's message.

Keep persistence separate from the model's context window. You can retain a conversation in Postgres while sending only selected messages or a summary to the model. Decide retention and deletion behavior for customer conversations before the app starts collecting sensitive text.

To add a rating to a saved answer, use the [assistant feedback storage guide](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/ai-assistant-feedback). It covers one vote per user and message, ownership checks and repeat submissions.

payload.content:
## [Which hosting setup fits the assistant?](https://www.prisma.io#which-hosting-setup-fits-the-assistant)

These options are ordered alphabetically by app host.

| App host | When to choose it | Database and response work | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify + Prisma Postgres | Your framework already uses [Netlify's deployment workflow](https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/create-deploys/). | Deploy the server features too, set the database URL in server configuration and check the runtime limits for your model calls. | 
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | You want the TypeScript server and database declared in one project. | Configure the Composer module, database dependency and model API secret. Check [request and streaming behavior](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout). | 
| Vercel + Prisma Postgres | Your app already follows Vercel's framework workflow. | Its [streaming function documentation](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/streaming-functions) explains response delivery; the app must still save conversation data. | 

Place the database-calling server [near Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/nodejs-database-regions). Changing app hosts is optional: Prisma Postgres accepts ordinary PostgreSQL connections from a supported server runtime.

Run this SQL in a fresh development database through its [direct connection](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database), then adapt the schema into your migration workflow. The account ID is illustrative; a real app should connect it to the authenticated account model.

payload.content:
## [3. Read history through an authorized endpoint](https://www.prisma.io#3-read-history-through-an-authorized-endpoint)

The demonstration account is `42`. This query joins the conversation's ownership to its messages:

The inner query selects the latest 50 messages; the outer query puts that page in display order. For the two demonstration messages, it returns the user question followed by the assistant reply, with their IDs. In the server, bind query values as parameters and derive the authorized account from the verified session. Apply that check to writes and deletes too. If you use row-level security, configure the relevant roles and policies as well.

Use the smallest returned message ID as the cursor when requesting an older page. The demonstration page starts at ID `1`, so this next-page query correctly returns no older rows:

The application should bind the conversation, verified account and cursor as parameters. A new conversation loads the first query without a cursor; subsequent requests use the smallest ID from the previous page. If parallel generations need a strict conversational turn sequence, model that sequence explicitly; an insertion ID alone does not define the order in which concurrent work completes.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host a TypeScript AI assistant that saves conversations in Postgres? > [4. Define generation and interruption states](https://www.prisma.io#4-define-generation-and-interruption-states)
payload.content:
## [4. Define generation and interruption states](https://www.prisma.io#4-define-generation-and-interruption-states)

Save the user message before calling the model. Create an assistant message in `pending` state, then save its content and mark it `completed` when generation succeeds. Use distinct request keys for the user message and assistant reply, with duplicate-request handling in the server.

Decide how interrupted work becomes `failed` or resumes. Persist a start time or job identifier if you need a recovery process to find abandoned pending messages after a crash. Catching errors in a handler alone cannot update a row after the process has stopped.

For token-level resumption, persist chunks or events before relying on them as durable history. The [Open Chat walkthrough](https://www.prisma.io/blog/building-open-chat) describes an event-log design with Prisma Streams. Saving only the final response has a smaller implementation, but loses unsaved output if generation is interrupted.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host a TypeScript AI assistant that saves conversations in Postgres? > [5. Deploy and test a return visit](https://www.prisma.io#5-deploy-and-test-a-return-visit)
payload.content:
## [5. Deploy and test a return visit](https://www.prisma.io#5-deploy-and-test-a-return-visit)

For a project with a `build` script and the `module.ts` prepared in step 1, authenticate, build the app and deploy a separate review stage. Configure the project region through the [deployment setup](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/deploy) if it is not already set. These commands use the current [Prisma 8 release candidate CLI](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/release-status) explicitly, so an older project-local CLI is not selected:

Open the service URL returned by the deployment. Confirm that its database target is the intended review resource before applying migrations or testing writes. An externally supplied URL must point to a separate test database; changing the stage name does not isolate an external database by itself.

Prisma Compute runs deployed services on Bun, so check runtime-dependent packages. Its [request timeout](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout) gives a service 60 seconds to start responding; a response that has started streaming is not subject to that first-byte deadline.

Test a saved conversation after refreshing, signing out and signing back in. Verify that another account cannot read its messages. Interrupt a generation and check that the UI and database state match the recovery behavior you chose. Also rehearse deleting a conversation and its associated messages.

payload.content:
## [When should I choose a different setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-a-different-setup)

Prisma Compute currently does not host WebSocket servers. Use an HTTP streaming design it supports, or choose another app host if WebSocket server support is a requirement. Streaming an HTTP response also does not guarantee that an in-process generation job survives a restart or deployment.

Choose database hosting with the regions, extensions and recovery features your customer data requires. Prisma Postgres has [plan-dependent snapshots](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) and no point-in-time recovery yet (it is coming in November 2026). Keep long-term history, backups and model-provider costs as separate decisions when estimating the app's operating budget.

payload.section: TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting?
payload.content:
## TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting?

`streamText` or your provider's streaming API. Then check the host's limit for a streamed response. Vercel counts the whole stream against `maxDuration` (with fluid compute, the default for projects created since April 23, 2025: 300 seconds by default, up to 800 on Pro and Enterprise), Google Cloud Run's request timeout defaults to 5 minutes and goes up to 60, Netlify stops synchronous and streaming functions at 60 seconds, Railway allows 15 minutes while data keeps flowing, and Cloudflare Workers have no wall-clock limit while the client stays connected. Turn off proxy buffering, and move agent runs that take longer than your host allows into a background job. On [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute), a service has 60 seconds to send its first bytes, and a response that has started streaming is not cut off when it passes 60 seconds.

A chat request that waits for the full model answer fails in one of two ways. Either nothing appears until the whole answer has been generated, or the request ends with a timeout before any of it arrives. Long answers, reasoning models and tool calls make both worse, because the time until the last token grows while the user sees nothing. The fix is to stream the answer as the model produces it and to give the whole stream enough time on your host.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The fix below works on any host. The host and library limits on this page link to their documentation, checked on October 22, 2026.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [Which timeout are you hitting?](https://www.prisma.io#which-timeout-are-you-hitting)
payload.content:
## [Which timeout are you hitting?](https://www.prisma.io#which-timeout-are-you-hitting)

What the user sees, and when, points to the cause.

| What you see | Likely cause | Check | 
|---|---|---|
| Nothing for a while, then the whole answer at once | The handler waits for the full answer, or a proxy buffers the stream | Whether the route returns before the model finishes, and the proxy's buffering setting | 
| A `504` with `FUNCTION_INVOCATION_TIMEOUT` on Vercel | The invocation ran past its maximum duration, which includes streaming | `maxDuration` for the route and your plan's maximum | 
| The function stops after 10 to 60 seconds on Vercel | The project runs without fluid compute, so the limits in Vercel's current tables don't apply to it | Whether fluid compute is on in the project's Functions settings, then `maxDuration` | 
| The answer stops partway at the same time on every long reply | A limit on the total request time | The host's limit for a streamed response, in the table below | 
| A `504 Gateway Time-out` from `openresty` after about 60 seconds on Prisma Compute | No bytes were sent within 60 seconds | Whether the route sends something before the model's first token | 
| A Cloudflare `524` page | Cloudflare's proxy got no response from your server within its read timeout | Whether the response starts within 125 seconds | 
| The stream dies during a long tool call | An idle timeout between two chunks | Proxy read timeouts, such as nginx's 60-second default |

To tell a buffering proxy from a route that doesn't stream, call the route with [`curl -N`](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#-N), which turns off curl's own output buffering. If curl prints the answer in pieces and the browser shows it all at once, look at the proxy or the client code. A buffering proxy holds the response for curl too, so if curl waits, send the same request once through the proxy and once straight to the app, for example to its port on the server. If curl also waits on the direct request, the route itself isn't streaming.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [Why it happens](https://www.prisma.io#why-it-happens)
payload.content:
## [Why it happens](https://www.prisma.io#why-it-happens)

Chat code often starts with a call that resolves when the model has finished, such as the AI SDK's `generateText` or a provider call without streaming. The server can't send anything until that call returns, so the user's wait is the model's total generation time, and the host's request limit applies to all of it.

Streaming changes what the user waits for: the server returns a response at once and writes each token as the model produces it. It doesn't remove the host's limits. On [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration), the maximum duration "includes time spent processing the request and sending the response, including streamed responses." So a streamed answer that runs longer than the limit is still cut off.

A proxy in front of the server can undo streaming. [nginx](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html#proxy_buffering) buffers responses from the proxied server by default (`proxy_buffering on`), so the browser gets chunks in batches or at the end.

payload.content:
## [1. Stream the model's answer from the route](https://www.prisma.io#1-stream-the-models-answer-from-the-route)

With the AI SDK, `streamText` starts the model call, and `createUIMessageStreamResponse` with `toUIMessageStream` returns a streaming response that the `useChat` hook reads, as in the [Next.js quickstart](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/getting-started/nextjs-app-router). Older examples write the same response as `result.toUIMessageStreamResponse()`, which the [`streamText` reference](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/reference/ai-sdk-core/stream-text) still lists. This route was type-checked and run with `ai` 7.0.148 and `@ai-sdk/openai` 4.0.99:

Passing `req.signal` stops the model call, and the tokens it uses, when the user closes the tab. It also stops it when a proxy drops the connection or the user refreshes, and then the answer is lost. If you save answers, leave out `abortSignal` and call `result.consumeStream()` without awaiting it: generation then runs to the end after a disconnect, and the `onEnd` callback of `toUIMessageStream` can save the finished messages, as the AI SDK's [message persistence docs](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-ui/chatbot-message-persistence#handling-client-disconnects) show.

On the client, `useChat` from `@ai-sdk/react` posts to `/api/chat` and renders each message's `parts` as they arrive, as the [AI SDK quickstart](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/getting-started/nextjs-app-router) shows. Tutorials written for AI SDK 4 use `toDataStreamResponse()` and `handleSubmit`, which AI SDK 5 replaced ([migration guide](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/migration-guides/migration-guide-5-0)), so check the docs for the version in your `package.json` before copying code.

## [2. Or stream server-sent events without the AI SDK](https://www.prisma.io#2-or-stream-server-sent-events-without-the-ai-sdk)

A provider SDK can stream on its own. With the [OpenAI SDK](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/streaming-responses), `stream: true` returns an iterable of events, and the text arrives in `response.output_text.delta` events. This route forwards them as [server-sent events](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events), type-checked and run with `openai` 7.42.0:

The first comment line goes out before the model call starts, and the heartbeat sends another every 15 seconds while a long tool call or reasoning step produces no text. MDN describes comment lines as a way "to prevent connections from timing out." On the client, read `response.body` with a reader and append each `data:` line's text as it arrives.

payload.content:
## [3. Give the stream enough time on your host](https://www.prisma.io#3-give-the-stream-enough-time-on-your-host)

Compare your longest answer, including tool calls, with the limit for a streamed response on your host. These hosts are ordered alphabetically:

| Host | Before the first byte | A response that is streaming | 
|---|---|---|
| Cloudflare Workers | No separate limit | [No wall-clock limit](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#duration) while the client stays connected. CPU time is limited separately: 10 ms on Free, 30 seconds by default and up to 5 minutes on Paid; waiting on `fetch()` doesn't count. | 
| Google Cloud Run | Part of the request timeout | The [request timeout](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/request-timeout) is 5 minutes by default and can be raised to 60 minutes; long-running requests, [WebSocket streams](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/triggering/websockets) included, are subject to it. For more than 15 minutes, Google recommends retries and clients that can reconnect. | 
| Netlify Functions | Part of the function's limit | 60 seconds for [synchronous](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/configuration/) (not configurable) and [streaming](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/api/) functions. Background functions run for 15 minutes but answer the client with a `202` at once. | 
| Prisma Compute | [60 seconds](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout) | Not cut off when it passes 60 seconds. The docs advise keeping data flowing and having the client reconnect for anything long-lived. | 
| Railway | 5 minutes with no data | [15 minutes](https://docs.railway.com/networking/public-networking/specs-and-limits) if data keeps transferring; closed after 5 minutes with no data. |

payload.content:
## [4. Turn off buffering in proxies](https://www.prisma.io#4-turn-off-buffering-in-proxies)

If nginx sits in front of the app, turn off buffering for the chat route, or send `X-Accel-Buffering: no` from the route as the second example does. nginx's [`proxy_read_timeout`](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html#proxy_read_timeout) defaults to 60 seconds between two reads, so keep the heartbeat shorter than that or raise the timeout. The AI SDK route in step 1 sends no heartbeat: after its first event, nothing goes out until the model produces output, so raise `proxy_read_timeout` for it when a tool call or reasoning step can run longer than 60 seconds:

Behind Cloudflare's proxy, the server has to start responding within 125 seconds or the visitor gets a [`524` error](https://developers.cloudflare.com/support/troubleshooting/http-status-codes/cloudflare-5xx-errors/error-524/). Enterprise plans can raise that to 6,000 seconds. A route that returns its streaming response at once, with an early comment line, starts responding well inside that window.

payload.section: [5. Move long agent runs out of the request](https://www.prisma.io#5-move-long-agent-runs-out-of-the-request)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [5. Move long agent runs out of the request](https://www.prisma.io#5-move-long-agent-runs-out-of-the-request)
payload.content:
## [5. Move long agent runs out of the request](https://www.prisma.io#5-move-long-agent-runs-out-of-the-request)

An agent loop that can run longer than your host allows doesn't belong in one HTTP request. Save the job, start it in a worker or a background job, and have the browser follow its progress: poll an endpoint, reconnect to a stream that reads saved output, or use the AI SDK's [resumable streams](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-ui/chatbot-resume-streams). If you use resumable streams, don't pass the request's abort signal to the model call, because a disconnect would then cancel the generation the client wants to reconnect to. Add a separate stop endpoint for user cancellation, as the [AI SDK docs](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/troubleshooting/abort-breaks-resumable-streams) describe. Save the user's message before you call the model, so a dropped connection doesn't lose the question as well as the answer.

payload.section: [How to choose hosting for a streaming chat app](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-choose-hosting-for-a-streaming-chat-app)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [How to choose hosting for a streaming chat app](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-choose-hosting-for-a-streaming-chat-app)
payload.content:
## [How to choose hosting for a streaming chat app](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-choose-hosting-for-a-streaming-chat-app)

Pick the host by the longest answer you need to deliver and by the connections your app holds open:

- **Answers finish in a few minutes, and the app already runs on Vercel:** stream, and set `maxDuration` to cover the longest answer.
- **Answers or agent runs can take longer than a serverless limit:** a host with a longer request limit, such as Google Cloud Run (up to 60 minutes per request) or Railway (15 minutes per request while data flows), a long-running server on Render, Fly.io or a VM you run, or a background job that the browser follows.
- **The app needs WebSocket connections:** a host that runs a WebSocket server, such as [Railway](https://docs.railway.com/networking/public-networking/specs-and-limits), where WebSocket connections are exempt from the duration limits, [Render](https://render.com/docs/websocket), which doesn't enforce a maximum duration for them, or [Fly.io](https://fly.io/docs/networking/websockets/), whose proxy doesn't close idle WebSocket connections. On [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/websockets), a WebSocket connection closes when the function reaches its maximum duration.
- **Answers start streaming within 60 seconds but can run longer, and you want the server and its Postgres database in one project:** Prisma Compute with Prisma Postgres, covered next (no WebSocket servers today; support is planned for early 2027).

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [Where does Prisma Compute fit?](https://www.prisma.io#where-does-prisma-compute-fit)
payload.content:
## [Where does Prisma Compute fit?](https://www.prisma.io#where-does-prisma-compute-fit)

Prisma Compute fits a TypeScript chat endpoint that starts streaming within 60 seconds: its [request timeout](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout) applies only to the wait for the first bytes, so a streamed answer that runs longer is not cut off when it passes 60 seconds. [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) hosts TypeScript apps built for Node.js, Bun or Next.js, and deployed apps run on Bun. It doesn't require Prisma ORM or Prisma Postgres.

A Next.js app deploys with [Prisma Composer](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer)'s `nextjs` build adapter and `output: "standalone"`, as the [Next.js guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/frameworks/nextjs) shows, so the chat route stays a route handler. Keep the model's API key in the deployment's secret configuration, as the [secrets guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-app-secrets) describes. The 60 seconds are counted by Compute's ingress, so `maxDuration` and timeouts inside the route don't change them.

When the 60 seconds pass with nothing sent, the client gets a `504` and Compute cancels the request. Your code sees that as an aborted `req.signal`, not as an error in the logs. While a stream waits on the model, the instance uses little CPU but stays running, and the [pricing docs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/pricing) bill provisioned memory for that time and active CPU only while code runs. The Free plan includes 1M requests, 360 GB-hours of memory and 4 active vCPU-hours per month, with no credit card.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [Where does Prisma Compute fit?](https://www.prisma.io#where-does-prisma-compute-fit)
payload.content:
Conversations can live in [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres) in the same project. The [conversation history guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/ai-assistant-conversation-history) covers the schema and ownership checks, and the [AI SDK guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/integrations/ai-sdk) saves each chat from the stream's `onEnd` callback with Prisma ORM. Any Postgres client works.

Know the limits before you rely on it:

- Compute does not run WebSocket servers today; support is planned for early 2027. Stream over HTTP or server-sent events, or run the socket server on another host.
- The docs don't state a maximum length for a started stream. They say to keep data flowing rather than let it sit idle, and to have the client reconnect for anything long-lived ([streaming responses](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout#streaming-responses)), so send a heartbeat during long tool calls and use a background job the client reconnects to for agent runs.
- The 60 seconds include everything before the first byte. A route that awaits a slow tool call or a long reasoning step before sending anything gets a `504`, so send an early event first.
- Work after the response, with `waitUntil` or `KeepAwakeGuard`, is best effort. It keeps the instance awake, but it doesn't retry failures or continue through a restart or a new deployment ([Keeping instances awake](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/keeping-instances-awake)). Generation that continues after the browser disconnects, as with `consumeStream()`, is background work in this sense. An agent run that must finish needs saved progress and a separate trigger.

payload.content:
- Each service runs in one region, and Compute has no edge runtime ([Known limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations)). Pick the region nearest your users or your database.
- If your answers fit inside a serverless limit and the app already runs on Vercel or Netlify, moving hosts doesn't fix a timeout. Stream and set the limit where the app runs.

payload.content:
## [How to prevent it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it)

Stream from the first version of the chat route, even when answers are short, so a slower model delays the first token instead of the whole answer. Set an explicit limit on the model call below the host's limit, with the AI SDK's [`timeout` option](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/reference/ai-sdk-core/stream-text) or an [`AbortSignal.timeout()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal/timeout_static), so your code returns an error the client can show instead of a gateway page. On Prisma Compute, keep a timeout on work before the first byte under 60 seconds, for example 50, as the [request timeout docs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout#what-your-service-sees) advise. Log how long the first token and the full answer take, and compare the slowest answers with your host's limit before you add tools or switch to a slower model.

payload.content:
## [When this fix doesn't apply](https://www.prisma.io#when-this-fix-doesnt-apply)

If the error comes from the model provider, such as a `429` rate limit or a provider timeout, streaming and hosting changes won't help; check the provider's error and retry rules. If the browser gives up first, look for a client-side timeout in a `fetch` wrapper or HTTP client. And if the request fails in under a second, the route is erroring, not timing out: read the server logs before changing limits.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host an AI API that charges credits?
payload.content:
## How should I host an AI API that charges credits?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)fits a small team that wants its API, saved usage and deployment configuration in one project. Vercel or Netlify with Prisma Postgres can also fit an existing app. The host runs the API; your application must define reservations, retries, settlement and customer-visible balances.

A customer with ten credits can send two requests at the same time. If both handlers read ten and each decides to spend seven, a check in application memory can approve work the balance cannot cover. Choose the hosting workflow you like, then enforce admission in the database.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. Provider and PostgreSQL sources linked here were checked on October 22, 2026.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host an AI API that charges credits? > [What must the setup keep reliable?](https://www.prisma.io#what-must-the-setup-keep-reliable)
payload.content:
## [What must the setup keep reliable?](https://www.prisma.io#what-must-the-setup-keep-reliable)

Keep an account balance, a history of credit changes and a record for each logical AI request. The history explains the balance; the request record explains whether work is reserved, running, completed or awaiting reconciliation. Keep model usage and the pricing rule used for the charge with that record.

Derive the account from verified authentication and calculate the charge on the server. A browser or model response must not choose the account balance or its own price. An AI assistant can write the implementation, but tests must prove its behavior with concurrent requests, retries and failures.

Separate the prices you charge customers from the [infrastructure meters](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-hosting-cost-visibility). A model request can cause several database queries and an app response. Those costs need their own budget even when the customer's credit price is fixed.

## [Which app host should I choose?](https://www.prisma.io#which-app-host-should-i-choose)

These options are alphabetical by app host and can use Prisma Postgres.

|---|---|---|
| Netlify + Prisma Postgres | An app already using [Netlify's function workflow](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/overview/). | Credit admission, request state and recovery after a function stops. | 
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | A TypeScript API and its database described together through [Prisma Composer](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer). | Transactions, model-call deadlines and settlement of unfinished requests. | 
| Vercel + Prisma Postgres | A Next.js app already using [Vercel's server functions](https://vercel.com/docs/functions). | Credential scope, concurrency and the same credit accounting rules. | 

For a new TypeScript API, Compute gives the team a deployment declaration its coding agent can inspect while Postgres keeps balances outside the running process. Keep a working app host when its deployment workflow already suits the product.

## [1. Create a separate development ledger](https://www.prisma.io#1-create-a-separate-development-ledger)

Create a development Prisma Postgres database in [Console](https://console.prisma.io). Use fictional accounts and credits, separate from live customers. Prisma ORM is optional.

Apply schema migrations through the database's [direct connection](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database). Use its pooled URL for ordinary TCP application connections; the [Prisma Postgres serverless driver](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/serverless-driver) requires the direct URL. Define constraints for nonnegative balances, valid request states and unique account/request identifiers.

payload.content:
## [2. Prove the conditional balance change](https://www.prisma.io#2-prove-the-conditional-balance-change)

With `psql` installed, open a direct connection to the development database. Paste this SQL into one session:

The first update returns `remaining = 3`; another seven-credit debit then returns no rows. PostgreSQL rechecks an update's condition after a competing writer commits under its [default isolation level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html).

This demonstrates one admission rule, not a complete credit ledger. The second update is another debit attempt, not a deduplicated retry. Production code needs saved request identifiers, transaction boundaries and a policy for database errors. The temporary table disappears when the session ends.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host an AI API that charges credits? > [3. Reserve, call the model and settle](https://www.prisma.io#3-reserve-call-the-model-and-settle)
payload.content:
## [3. Reserve, call the model and settle](https://www.prisma.io#3-reserve-call-the-model-and-settle)

For an implemented ledger, make the sequence explicit:

1. Authenticate the account and assign or reuse the logical request ID.
2. Start a transaction, lock the account's wallet row, and look up the request by account and request ID. If it exists, compare the validated inputs and any client-requested credit limit with its saved inputs or fingerprint; reject a mismatch. For a matching retry, end the transaction and return the saved state under its original pricing rules. For a new request, check the balance and persist the validated inputs and model/work limits, or an immutable durable reference to them. Save a canonical fingerprint and the server-decided credit amount and pricing version, reserve the credits, mark the request reserved and add its credit-history entry in that same transaction, then commit. Roll back a rejected request.
3. Atomically claim the reserved request by changing its state to running, and commit that change before submitting it to the model. Only the process that won this transition may submit the call. Make the call outside the transaction with a deadline, and save the provider request identifier when it becomes available.
4. In a new transaction, conditionally change the request from an allowed unfinished state to its final state. Only the transaction that wins this transition may apply the settlement or release to the wallet and add the corresponding credit-history entry; commit those changes together. A retry that finds a final request returns its saved result, while other invalid transitions are rejected.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host an AI API that charges credits? > [3. Reserve, call the model and settle](https://www.prisma.io#3-reserve-call-the-model-and-settle)
payload.content:
When a model call times out, its outcome may be uncertain. Keep that request in a state your reconciliation process can inspect rather than immediately refunding and sending the same expensive work again. A database transaction cannot make an external API call happen exactly once.

Deploy a recovery worker that periodically finds reservations whose processing deadline has passed. A still-reserved request can be claimed through the same atomic transition. An expired running request is uncertain until the provider confirms its outcome, even when no provider identifier was saved: the process may have stopped after submission. Do not automatically release its credits or resubmit it. Check the provider's result or usage records when available; otherwise hold the reservation for an explicit review policy. The [Postgres worker guide](https://www.prisma.io/blog/you-dont-need-a-job-queue-postgres-already-has-skip-locked#where-to-run-the-worker) explains the always-on host needed for a polling process. Saving a reservation alone does not schedule its recovery.

For variable-cost work, reserve an explicit upper bound and enforce the corresponding model-output or work limit. Define what happens when a request reaches it. Fixed-price credits need a different settlement rule from pass-through token pricing.

payload.content:
## [4. Deploy and test the whole request lifecycle](https://www.prisma.io#4-deploy-and-test-the-whole-request-lifecycle)

Follow [Compute getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started), or [port the existing API](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/porting-an-app), to configure the server and its inputs. Keep model keys in server-side secret configuration.

A database created by a Composer module is separate from a Console-created development database. Prepare every review and production target through the [migration workflow](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/production-database-migrations) before serving customer work. A configured `postgres()` data contract can apply migrations during deployment; `rawPostgres()` and manually supplied URLs require your own migration step.

Test simultaneous requests, repeated IDs, insufficient credits, a model failure, a timeout after success and a process restart between reservation and settlement. An API response and the customer's usage screen should agree with the saved request state.

payload.content:
## [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)

Choose a billing service if you need an existing product to own subscriptions, credit expiry or invoicing rules. If Stripe funds the wallet, verify payment events and deduplicate top-ups; the [Stripe hosting guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/nextjs-stripe-subscriptions) covers that boundary.

Compute has [60 seconds to start a response](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout). Long-running requests need a suitable durable worker design, not an in-memory promise treated as a queue. Check the runtime and recovery requirements before selecting the worker host. Prisma Postgres has [automatic snapshots on paid plans, created daily on days with database activity](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups), with no point-in-time recovery yet (it is coming in November 2026); choose another database if you need that recovery window today.
