## How can I check my app and database in one place?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)gives a TypeScript team one project to inspect through Console and the CLI, with Query Insights for database behavior. Use an external check of a real application route as well: an available service and a reachable database do not prove that sign-in or saving a record works.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)8 min read

A dashboard can show a running server while customers see an error. The server may have the wrong database credentials, an unapplied schema change or a broken login callback. A useful hosting setup helps you tell those failures apart.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. Provider documentation linked here was checked on October 22, 2026. Prisma ORM is optional.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How can I check my app and database in one place? > [Which checks answer which question?](https://www.prisma.io#which-checks-answer-which-question)
payload.content:
## [Which checks answer which question?](https://www.prisma.io#which-checks-answer-which-question)

Keep process availability, dependency readiness and customer success separate. That distinction makes an alert actionable.

| Check | What it tells you | What it leaves untested | 
|---|---|---|
| A small HTTP response without a database query | The service can answer a request. | Database access, authentication and saved records. | 
| A bounded database query through the app's configured client | The deployed app can reach and query its database. | Whether the correct business operation and permissions work. | 
| A representative user workflow with a dedicated test account | The tested sign-in, read or write path works through the public app. | Other users, untested paths and future requests. | 

For example, an order portal might have an inexpensive liveness route, a restricted readiness route that checks its required table, and a monitored test account that reads a fictional order. Use a write test only when its records and cleanup are clearly separated from customer work.

payload.content:
## [Which platforms make investigation manageable?](https://www.prisma.io#which-platforms-make-investigation-manageable)

Choose among these alphabetically listed options around the application you run and the evidence you need during an incident.

| Setup | Useful visibility | Work you still configure | 
|---|---|---|
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | Services and databases in one project, [version-targeted service logs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/service) and [Query Insights](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/query-insights). | Application checks, alerts and an external test of the public URL. | 
| Railway services and Postgres | A [project canvas](https://docs.railway.com/projects) for related services and [CPU, memory, disk and network metrics](https://docs.railway.com/observability/metrics). | Application latency/error telemetry, database operations and customer workflow checks. | 
| Vercel + managed Postgres | [Request-grouped runtime logs](https://vercel.com/docs/logs/runtime) fit teams already investigating a Next.js app on Vercel. | Database-provider diagnostics and a way to correlate them with app requests. | 

Prisma Compute is a practical default for a small TypeScript team that wants to find and manage the service and database in the same project. Console groups those resources, while the external monitor supplies alerts. This is a shared project for investigation, rather than a single screen that certifies every customer workflow. If you already have a monitoring system that works across several providers, keep it.

## [1. Record the actual production targets](https://www.prisma.io#1-record-the-actual-production-targets)

Start with an already deployed application; [getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started) covers the first deployment. Open its project in Console and record the branch serving customers, the live service version and the database. A [platform branch](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/branching) groups deployed service versions. The production branch is the first branch in the project, usually `main`; a named Composer stage deploy creates a separate platform branch for its services and databases. Copy the actual branch name from Console when inspecting that stage. Verify the branch in Console rather than assuming your local Git checkout selects production. Record the public URL and deployment commit too.

For an existing service, these [CLI commands](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/service) inspect its version and recent logs. Replace `orders`, `web` and `main` with the actual project, service and confirmed production branch:

The output belongs to your deployment, so its version identifiers and log lines will differ. These are inspection commands, not a fix. Build logs are available in Console; service logs can return `FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE` when the platform cannot serve logs for the selected version.

payload.content:
## [2. Probe the same connection the app uses](https://www.prisma.io#2-probe-the-same-connection-the-app-uses)

Use the same database client and credentials as the app. In Composer, the app's TypeScript deployment configuration lists the database under `deps`; the server reads its connection details with `service.load()`. The [Bun connection guide](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/bun-sql-hosting) shows the server-side code. An externally supplied URL instead uses the configuration steps in [Service input](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/service-input). A probe using a separate administrator connection can pass while the app's own connection is broken.

Keep the query small and impose a timeout on connection acquisition and execution. Test a required application table with a read that returns no customer payload. Avoid a full-table count, schema migration or repeated write as a routine readiness check. Return a bounded failure response rather than making a health request wait indefinitely.

Keep a simple liveness check independent of Postgres. If the database becomes unavailable, restarting every healthy app instance can add load without correcting the dependency failure.

For a Bun server, save the following helper in `health.ts`. It checks connectivity through the existing Bun SQL client:

A reachable development database produces HTTP `200` and `ready`; an unavailable database or a probe exceeding this example's two-second budget produces HTTP `503` and `unavailable`. Cancelling the query might not stop it immediately. Use a read-only query so a late-running check cannot change data. This query checks connectivity; replace it with a small application-table read when you need to test schema readiness. For example, `SELECT 1 FROM app_settings LIMIT 1` verifies that a table can be queried without returning its contents; replace the example table name with a required table in your schema and adjust the success test to accept an empty result. Keep the existing liveness route free of database work.

payload.content:
Integrate this with the existing server rather than replacing its application routes. The following wrapper accepts the existing request handler, SQL client and monitor token, and forwards only the two health paths to the adapter:

Save the adapter as `health-handler.ts` and the wrapper as `with-health-routes.ts`. Set the existing `Bun.serve` call's `fetch` option to `withHealthRoutes(appHandler, sql, monitorToken)`, importing the wrapper into that server file. Here `appHandler` is the app's current handler and `sql` is its current client. On Compute, follow [Service input](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/service-input) to declare a monitor-token configuration field in `service.ts`, name its secret platform variable with `envSecret(...)` in `module.ts`, and read its value on the server. Pass that secret's exposed string as `monitorToken`. The monitor sends `Authorization: Bearer <the configured token>`; a missing or wrong value must produce `401`, never a database diagnostic.

payload.content:
## [3. Correlate an outside-in check with the diagnostics](https://www.prisma.io#3-correlate-an-outside-in-check-with-the-diagnostics)

Run a check from outside the hosting platform against the intended public URL. Confirm that it reaches the application rather than a cached static response or a login redirect that always returns success. A dedicated test account can exercise authentication and one representative saved-data read.

For example, Better Stack documents [creating an API monitor with an authentication header](https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/api-monitor/) and [choosing notification channels](https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/monitoring-start/). Set the deployed readiness URL, supply the dedicated monitor credential through its request headers, choose the expected success status and timeout, and select an actual responder. Test the failure notification before relying on it. This HTTP check covers the readiness route; a customer journey needs an additional authenticated workflow test.

Configure the monitor to send an `X-Monitor-Id` header identifying that monitor, and record that header with the request timestamp in the server's access logs so you can match failed probes to activity. Record the live deployment version from `service show` alongside the monitor result. In [Prisma Console](https://console.prisma.io), open the affected project's database and its [Query Insights](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/query-insights) view. Compare query latency and repeated SQL in the failure's time window with service logs. Slow SQL calls for query investigation; a request that never reaches SQL calls for a different investigation.

payload.content:
## [4. Test the alert and its operating cost](https://www.prisma.io#4-test-the-alert-and-its-operating-cost)

In an [isolated review environment](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/typescript-test-environment), temporarily pass the health adapter a separate Bun SQL client with a deliberately invalid test connection URL. This tests failure handling without changing the database connection supplied by Composer. Verify that the dependency check fails, the liveness route still explains whether the server responds, and an alert reaches the channel your team actually watches. Restore the test configuration afterward.

Before applying the configuration to production, review the interval, timeout, access control and [usage cost](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-hosting-cost-visibility). Prisma Compute meters requests and active resources, and Prisma Postgres meters operations. A probe should earn the work it causes, especially for an app used only occasionally.

## [When is a different setup a better fit?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-a-different-setup-a-better-fit)

Use an existing cross-provider observability system when you need unified tracing across many services or organizations. Console and CLI inspection are not a substitute for that requirement, and a platform status page cannot certify your application's business rules.

Check [Compute's current limits](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations) for log availability and runtime requirements. Do not choose a host on the assumption that retaining an open connection, an in-memory monitor or a local file will survive a redeploy. Keep the check's state and alerting outside the process it is checking.

## Where should I host my exported Bolt or Lovable app?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)fits a TypeScript server that owns its database queries and should deploy with its database in one project. Vercel or Netlify can suit an exported frontend or a supported full-stack framework. If the app already uses Supabase authentication, storage or browser database APIs, keep that backend for the first deployment and plan a separate migration when you need one.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)7 min read

An exported customer portal might contain a frontend, server routes and calls to a managed backend. Getting its repository onto another host is one task. Moving the customer accounts, documents and data that those calls depend on is another.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The official sources linked here were checked on October 29, 2026. Bolt and Lovable both provide their own publishing workflows; keeping a working deployment there is a reasonable choice when source ownership is your main concern and you do not need to change hosts.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host my exported Bolt or Lovable app? > [What did the builder actually export?](https://www.prisma.io#what-did-the-builder-actually-export)
payload.content:
## [What did the builder actually export?](https://www.prisma.io#what-did-the-builder-actually-export)

Inspect the repository before choosing a deployment preset. Read its package scripts, framework configuration, server entry points, environment-variable names and backend SDK imports. Have your assistant list the services each feature calls, rather than describe the project only as a React app.

[Lovable's external-hosting guide](https://docs.lovable.dev/tips-tricks/external-deployment-hosting) distinguishes newer TanStack Start apps from older React and Vite apps. The former include a server part; the latter can build to static frontend files. A static-file deployment cannot execute server functions simply because the landing page loads.

[Bolt's Git integration](https://support.bolt.new/integrations/git) provides a source-control path, and its [project-management guide](https://support.bolt.new/managing-projects/projects-files) covers downloading a project. Check the exported application rather than assuming that every Bolt project has the same framework or database arrangement.

Make a short inventory for your app:

| Part | Evidence to inspect | Deployment consequence | 
|---|---|---|
| Browser frontend | Its build output, routing and public configuration. | Static output needs hosting and route handling; server-rendered output also needs a server runtime. | 
| Server code | API routes, server functions, webhooks and private keys. | Deploy these to a compatible runtime and recreate their server-side secrets. | 
| Backend services | Database SDK calls, auth redirects, file buckets, functions and realtime subscriptions. | Preserve those services or implement and test their replacements. |

## [Which hosting setup should I choose?](https://www.prisma.io#which-hosting-setup-should-i-choose)

The hosts below are ordered alphabetically. Keep the existing backend during an initial frontend move when that avoids changing two systems at once.

| App host | Useful fit | What you manage | 
|---|---|---|
| [Netlify](https://docs.netlify.com/build/frameworks/overview/) | A frontend or full-stack framework supported by its deployment adapter. | Build settings, the framework's server support, environment variables, route behavior and the connection to the existing backend or a separate API. | 
| Prisma Compute | You want a TypeScript application server and its Postgres dependency declared together, with CLI-driven deployment and inspection. | The Composer declaration, a build compatible with Bun, application authorization, migrations and any backend services you replace. No WebSocket servers or persistent writable filesystem. See [limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations). | 
| [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/frameworks) | An exported app whose framework matches its supported build and server deployment path. | Framework configuration, server execution limits, environment variables, authentication callbacks and the database or backend connection. | 

Prisma's integration is useful once your team owns the server's business logic: the service and database dependency live in the same declaration, so an assistant can inspect their relationship while deploying or debugging. [Composer's plain Postgres path](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases) supports the database client you already use; Prisma ORM is optional.

payload.content:
## [1. Establish a working export](https://www.prisma.io#1-establish-a-working-export)

Export or sync the repository, keep its lockfile, and run its documented production build in a clean local checkout as a validation step. Inspect the output and start procedure. For server-rendered apps, follow the framework's deployment adapter rather than treating the build output as a directory of static pages.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host my exported Bolt or Lovable app? > [2. Recreate configuration deliberately](https://www.prisma.io#2-recreate-configuration-deliberately)
payload.content:
## [2. Recreate configuration deliberately](https://www.prisma.io#2-recreate-configuration-deliberately)

Set the public backend configuration before the new host runs its deployment build. For example, a Vite app embeds values such as `VITE_SUPABASE_URL` in the browser bundle at build time; changing those values requires rebuilding and redeploying. Recreate private secrets in the new server environment. Builder-managed secrets are not something to recover from Git. Keep database passwords, payment secrets and privileged backend keys out of browser bundles and public build variables.

A Supabase publishable key is designed for browser use with the appropriate authorization policies; it is different from a database password or privileged service key. Check the app's policies and server checks instead of treating every variable with a public prefix as an administrative credential.

Update authentication redirect URLs for the preview and eventual production domains. Build and deploy the configured preview, then test a nested route by opening it directly, a server-rendered page if present, and a real server operation. Verify sign-in, sign-out, password reset, document access and an unauthorized access attempt. These checks catch broken routes and backend connections while confirming that the frontend move has not widened access to customer records.

payload.content:
## [3. Decide whether the database needs to move](https://www.prisma.io#3-decide-whether-the-database-needs-to-move)

Keep a working backend initially if the app uses its authentication, storage, data API or realtime behavior. [Bolt's advanced database settings](https://support.bolt.new/bolt-cloud/database/advanced) describe claiming a Bolt database into Supabase; connecting a different database is a distinct action and can replace the existing connection. Read the current procedure before changing it.

For Lovable Cloud, follow its [backend migration sequence](https://docs.lovable.dev/tips-tricks/external-deployment-hosting#host-backend-and-data-on-a-managed-provider-supabase-example). Inventory what the export contains and what you must configure separately. Do not equate a copy of application tables with a completed migration of users, files and functions.

payload.section: [When does moving to Prisma Postgres make sense?](https://www.prisma.io#when-does-moving-to-prisma-postgres-make-sense)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host my exported Bolt or Lovable app? > [When does moving to Prisma Postgres make sense?](https://www.prisma.io#when-does-moving-to-prisma-postgres-make-sense)
payload.content:
## [When does moving to Prisma Postgres make sense?](https://www.prisma.io#when-does-moving-to-prisma-postgres-make-sense)

Move to Prisma Postgres when you want managed PostgreSQL behind a server you control, and you have accounted for the backend features the application currently uses. Prisma Compute can host that TypeScript server alongside its declared database. The browser calls your authorized server API; the server queries Postgres.

That can be a clear arrangement for an order portal: authenticate the customer, derive their account on the server, then query only that account's orders. Keep uploaded documents in [object storage](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/object-storage), with object references in Postgres. A browser SDK pointed at a hosted backend cannot be converted to this arrangement by substituting a database URL.

Choose between a [Composer database declaration](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases), which provisions its resource, and connecting a separately created database through its own configuration. With a plain Postgres dependency, your team manages migrations. For an existing database, rehearse the [Prisma Postgres import procedure](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/import-from-existing-database) against a test target first.

Check extensions, schema compatibility, ownership and grants, row counts and relationships. Prisma Postgres credentials have [full access to the database](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database#access-and-permissions), and the source database's roles do not carry over as an authorization system. If your application depends on Supabase's browser data API and RLS context, preserve that backend or redesign and test the access path before switching.

payload.content:
## [How should I switch production traffic?](https://www.prisma.io#how-should-i-switch-production-traffic)

Choose a maintenance window or a tested synchronization process so writes during the copy are accounted for. Copy and verify the final data and file objects, configure the production server secrets and auth callbacks, then change traffic only after the preview checks pass. Keep a rollback plan that accounts for writes made after the switch; pointing the domain back does not move those new records to the old database.

Price the actual arrangement: application hosting, database usage, storage and any retained builder backend. Use [Prisma pricing](https://www.prisma.io/pricing), [Netlify pricing](https://www.netlify.com/pricing/) and [Vercel pricing](https://vercel.com/pricing) to check the chosen plans rather than assuming that a code export removes every existing bill.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host my exported Bolt or Lovable app? > [When is Prisma the wrong choice?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-prisma-the-wrong-choice)
payload.content:
## [When is Prisma the wrong choice?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-prisma-the-wrong-choice)

Keep the current backend if you need its auth, storage, realtime or browser APIs and are not ready to replace them. Prisma Postgres alone does not supply those application services. Choose another runtime if a dependency cannot run under Bun, and another hosting arrangement for a WebSocket server or persistent local filesystem. Those are [Compute limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations), not build settings an assistant can wish away.

For valuable customer data, check [backup and recovery behavior](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) before cutting over. Paid Prisma plans provide daily snapshots on days with database activity; point-in-time recovery is not available. Choose a provider with the recovery guarantees your business requires if losing changes since a snapshot is unacceptable.

payload.content:
## What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)is a practical fit for an AI-built TypeScript business app because its services and database live in one project, with a Console and CLI your assistant can help inspect. You can manage routine operations as the owner, but the application still needs someone responsible for authentication, code changes and recovery.

The first question is what you expect to manage. Checking a live URL, reviewing a bill and approving a tested release are reasonable owner tasks. Diagnosing an authorization flaw or recovering corrupted business records may need experienced technical help. A managed platform removes server administration from that list, while application ownership stays with the business.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The vendor sources linked below were checked on October 20, 2026. This guide is for an existing TypeScript app; it does not assume that hosting turns custom software into a maintained business product.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer? > [What should the platform take care of?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-the-platform-take-care-of)
payload.content:
## [What should the platform take care of?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-the-platform-take-care-of)

Look for a repeatable deployment process, an identifiable live version, accessible logs and a managed database. Keep the hosting account, source repository, domain and billing under business-controlled ownership. A contractor's personal account should not be the only route to your customer records.

Your assistant should be able to explain how the app is built, where data is saved and how a release is checked. Put the deployment declaration and migrations in the repository so future help can inspect them. Store credentials in a password manager and server-side secret configuration, with a recovery path that survives someone's departure.

payload.content:
## [Which hosting approach fits this situation?](https://www.prisma.io#which-hosting-approach-fits-this-situation)

These app hosts are ordered alphabetically. All require you to maintain your own application code.

| Approach | Good fit | Owner's next check | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify + managed Postgres | An existing app already uses its [Git deployments and framework integration](https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/deploy-overview/). | Confirm who owns the database account and how server functions receive its credentials. | 
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | A TypeScript app whose server and database you want in one project, inspectable through [Console and CLI](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started). | Have the app's Composer declaration, environment inputs and recovery procedure explained at handoff. | 
| Vercel + managed Postgres | A Next.js app already built around [Vercel's deployment workflow](https://vercel.com/docs/deployments). | Verify access to production deployments and the separate database's backups and billing. | 

Prisma Compute gives a small team a concrete TypeScript deployment definition for its agent to read and change. Prisma Postgres accepts ordinary PostgreSQL clients, so an existing app can keep its database library. For an owner who wants a finished tool maintained by its vendor, compare a hosted business application or a supported app builder instead of starting with a custom repository.

payload.content:
## [1. Establish ownership and a release boundary](https://www.prisma.io#1-establish-ownership-and-a-release-boundary)

Use [getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started) to prepare a Composer app and a managed database. Ask whoever prepares the app to demonstrate the build, an [isolated review deployment](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/deploying#production-and-stages) using a named stage such as `--stage review`, and a separate production release. Define which changes you can approve yourself and who handles failures you cannot diagnose.

Keep reviews on [separate test data](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/typescript-test-environment). If the app receives a manually supplied database URL, configure the test and production values separately. A test deployment connected to the production database can still change customer records.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer? > [2. Keep a short operations record](https://www.prisma.io#2-keep-a-short-operations-record)
payload.content:
## [2. Keep a short operations record](https://www.prisma.io#2-keep-a-short-operations-record)

Record the project, production branch, service name, live URL, database identity and the repository commit for the current release. Add a representative business test, such as signing in and saving a fictional booking, plus its cleanup procedure. Record where errors go and who can help; do not paste secret values into this document.

After CLI login using the current [supported runtime](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations#cli), the owner or assistant can inspect an existing project:

Here `business-portal`, `main` and `web` stand for your actual project, confirmed production branch and service name returned by the list. These commands inspect resources; they do not deploy or write customer data. The [service reference](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/service) explains the returned live-version details. Use `@latest` deliberately for the hosting CLI; it does not require upgrading the app's installed ORM.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer? > [3. Decide what recovery means](https://www.prisma.io#3-decide-what-recovery-means)
payload.content:
## [3. Decide what recovery means](https://www.prisma.io#3-decide-what-recovery-means)

Set a tolerable amount of lost work and a tolerable recovery time. A database snapshot from yesterday may be unacceptable if today's orders cannot be reconstructed. Prisma Postgres [backups](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) depend on the plan, and point-in-time recovery is not available until November 2026. Choose the provider and plan around the business requirement.

Rehearse restoration into a separate database and check that the application can read it. Keep exports where appropriate, and verify that the business can reach the credentials needed to recover. A backup entry in a dashboard is less useful than a restoration procedure someone has tested.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer? > [4. Review usage and changes regularly](https://www.prisma.io#4-review-usage-and-changes-regularly)
payload.content:
## [4. Review usage and changes regularly](https://www.prisma.io#4-review-usage-and-changes-regularly)

Use the current [pricing and plan limits](https://www.prisma.io/pricing) to set a budget, and understand what happens when a limit stops service. Paid-plan spending controls and free-plan quotas protect different things; neither proves that the app will stay available under every workload.

Review failed requests, dependency updates and access changes as part of operating the app. Test updates before release and retain the previous working version and its compatible schema. The [deployment handoff guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/deployment-handoff-checks) gives a practical acceptance check.

For checks that distinguish a running process from a working customer flow, use the [app and database health guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/app-database-health-checks). It connects service inspection, bounded database checks and an external test of the public app.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer? > [When is this the wrong setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-this-the-wrong-setup)
payload.content:
## [When is this the wrong setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-this-the-wrong-setup)

Choose a maintained business product if you need someone else to own both hosting and the application's ongoing behavior. An AI assistant can help with the work, but it does not create an accountable maintainer or guarantee that a proposed fix is correct.

Also check the [Compute runtime limits](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations). Deployed services run on Bun; WebSocket servers and a persistent writable filesystem are unsupported, and each service runs in one region. Keep Prisma Postgres with another app host when that host better fits a required runtime or operating workflow.

Before relying on the backup policy, [practice restoring a hosted Postgres database](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/practice-database-recovery) into an isolated target and verify the application against the recovered records.

## Which hosting service can Cursor help set up for my TypeScript app?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)is a strong fit when you want the TypeScript app and

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)in one project, using a deployment declaration your assistant can edit. Vercel and Netlify are also practical choices for apps already built around their framework integrations. Choose the host for your app's runtime, then let Cursor help with its setup.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)6 min read

The useful question is whether your assistant can inspect the deployment configuration, run the build and tell you what failed. A host's CLI, documented configuration files and readable logs make that work possible. Your editor does not need a special partnership with the host for its terminal to run a deployment command.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The official documentation linked below was checked on October 17, 2026. Prisma ORM is optional; choosing Prisma hosting does not require rewriting database access to use it.

payload.section: [What should Cursor inspect before choosing a host?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-cursor-inspect-before-choosing-a-host)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting service can Cursor help set up for my TypeScript app? > [What should Cursor inspect before choosing a host?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-cursor-inspect-before-choosing-a-host)
payload.content:
## [What should Cursor inspect before choosing a host?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-cursor-inspect-before-choosing-a-host)

Ask Cursor to identify the framework, package manager, build command, server entry point and database client from your project. Have it report whether the app needs long-running processes, WebSocket connections, scheduled work or writable local files. These requirements decide which runtime can run the app.

It should also find where configuration comes from without printing secret values. A working local `.env` file does not configure the deployment environment. An app that uses an in-memory array or browser storage may need a [persistent database](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/prototype-customer-data) before it can support real customers.

Cursor's [Agent documentation](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/overview) describes its code editing and terminal tools. Review the proposed file changes and resource targets before authorizing commands that affect an account.

payload.content:
## [Which hosting workflows can it help with?](https://www.prisma.io#which-hosting-workflows-can-it-help-with)

These options are ordered alphabetically by host name.

| App host | Useful project workflow | What to check first | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify | Configure the build and use its [CLI or Git deployment workflow](https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/create-deploys/). | Your framework's server features must be supported by the deployment integration. A frontend upload does not deploy an arbitrary backend process. | 
| Prisma Compute | Edit the TypeScript Composer module, build the app and use the [Prisma deployment CLI](https://www.prisma.io/docs/prisma-compute/deploy). | The app must fit the deployed Bun runtime and [supported features](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations). Declare the services, database dependencies and inputs explicitly. | 
| Vercel | Link the project and use its [CLI preview deployment workflow](https://vercel.com/docs/projects/deploy-from-cli). | Confirm the framework configuration, function runtime and separate Preview and Production environment variables. | 

A Prisma Composer module is a TypeScript file that declares the app's services, database dependencies and environment inputs. Prisma Compute keeps this file alongside application code. That gives Cursor concrete files to review when a dependency or environment input changes. Prisma's [MCP server](https://www.prisma.io/docs/ai/tools/mcp-server) can also expose account resources and diagnostic tools after you authorize the connection.

## [2. Connect MCP if you want its tools](https://www.prisma.io#2-connect-mcp-if-you-want-its-tools)

Follow [Cursor's MCP configuration documentation](https://cursor.com/docs/mcp) and Prisma's [MCP setup guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/ai/tools/mcp-server). For a project configuration at `.cursor/mcp.json`, the hosted Prisma endpoint is:

## [3. Prepare and build the application](https://www.prisma.io#3-prepare-and-build-the-application)

Follow the [framework-specific deployment instructions](https://www.prisma.io/docs/prisma-compute/deploy) to define a Composer module, configure its inputs and produce the required artifact. Server processes must listen on the assigned service port and `0.0.0.0`. Run the app's tests and build locally before uploading it.

Declare the review database using the [Composer database dependency guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases), or supply a separately managed test database URL as a server-side input. For a declared dependency named `db`, the server receives its connection through `service.load().db.url`. Keep other secrets in server-side inputs. If you use manually configured connection strings, verify them independently: the deployment's name does not prove that its URL points to a test database.

From the project containing the prepared module and built artifacts, use the Prisma CLI. For a module called `module.ts`:

## [5. Make future changes repeatable](https://www.prisma.io#5-make-future-changes-repeatable)

Commit the deployment declaration and migration files with the app. Keep secrets out of Git. If you want deployments on Git pushes, follow the [GitHub deployment setup](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/deployments) rather than assuming the first CLI deployment enables it. Decide which branches may change production and how migrations will run.

payload.content:
## [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)

Choose another host if required dependencies need a runtime feature outside Prisma Compute's supported environment. For example, it does not provide a persistent writable filesystem or host WebSocket servers. Customer uploads belong in object storage on any host; see [where to store files that disappear after a redeploy](https://www.prisma.io/compute/file-uploads-disappear-after-redeploy). You can still use Prisma Postgres from another application host.

If the app already deploys correctly to Netlify or Vercel, improving that configuration can be less work than migrating. Cursor can help with those CLIs too. Restricting credentials and account access matters on every host: a natural-language instruction to avoid production is useful context, but it is not an account permission boundary.

For database provisioning choices specifically, see [Postgres providers Codex can provision through tools or an API](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/codex-database-provisioning). That guide distinguishes infrastructure credentials from the application's database connection.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure?
payload.content:
## Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute), a custom domain is one CNAME on a production app, and Prisma Compute verifies the DNS record and provisions the certificate.

[Gregory Boch](https://github.com/gregory-boch-prisma)7 min read

When the generated URL (`your-app.example-host.com`) works and your own domain does not, the app itself is running. A request to your domain fails before it reaches the app, or it reaches the app with a name the app does not expect. The fix is configuration in three places: the host's domain settings, your DNS provider and the app itself.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The other providers' documentation linked on this page was checked on October 19, 2026.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [Which layer is failing?](https://www.prisma.io#which-layer-is-failing)
payload.content:
## [Which layer is failing?](https://www.prisma.io#which-layer-is-failing)

What the browser shows on your domain points to the layer to fix. Run the checks against your own hostname.

| What you see on your domain | Likely cause | Check | 
|---|---|---|
| "Site can't be reached", `NXDOMAIN` | No DNS record, or a typo in its name | `dig +short app.example.com` returns nothing | 
| A registrar parking page or an old site | An old record still answers, or the new one hasn't propagated | `dig +short app.example.com` returns an address you don't recognize | 
| A 404 page or error page from the host | DNS points at the host, but the domain isn't added to your app | The domain is missing or unverified in the host's settings | 
| A certificate warning | No certificate has been issued for your domain yet | The domain status in the host's dashboard or CLI | 
| "Too many redirects" | A proxy and the app redirect between HTTP and HTTPS | The proxy's TLS mode and the app's redirect rules | 
| The page loads, but login, API calls or sessions fail | The app still uses the old URL | Base URL, OAuth redirect URIs, CORS origins, cookie domain |

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [Why it happens](https://www.prisma.io#why-it-happens)
payload.content:
## [Why it happens](https://www.prisma.io#why-it-happens)

A hosting platform serves many apps from shared infrastructure and decides which app gets a request from the hostname in that request. Your domain only reaches your app when three things line up. DNS has to send the name to the host, the host has to know the name belongs to your app, and the host needs a TLS certificate issued for that exact name. The generated URL already has all three, which is why it works.

The fourth gap is inside the app. Code and settings written while the app lived at the generated URL often hard-code that URL. Redirects, OAuth callbacks, API calls from the browser and cookies then keep pointing at the old name.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [How to fix it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-fix-it)
payload.content:
## [How to fix it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-fix-it)

These steps work on any host. Replace `app.example.com` with your hostname and use the record values your host gives you.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [1. Add the domain in the host's settings](https://www.prisma.io#1-add-the-domain-in-the-hosts-settings)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [1. Add the domain in the host's settings](https://www.prisma.io#1-add-the-domain-in-the-hosts-settings)
payload.content:
## [1. Add the domain in the host's settings](https://www.prisma.io#1-add-the-domain-in-the-hosts-settings)

DNS alone does not attach a domain to an app. Add the exact hostname in the host's domain settings, and add `example.com` and `www.example.com` separately if you want both. [Vercel's troubleshooting guide](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/troubleshooting) starts with the same question: is the domain added to the project? Some hosts check DNS before they accept the domain, so the order of steps 1 and 2 depends on the host.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [2. Create the record the host asks for](https://www.prisma.io#2-create-the-record-the-host-asks-for)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [2. Create the record the host asks for](https://www.prisma.io#2-create-the-record-the-host-asks-for)
payload.content:
## [2. Create the record the host asks for](https://www.prisma.io#2-create-the-record-the-host-asks-for)

For a subdomain such as `app.example.com` or `www.example.com`, create a CNAME record whose value is the target the host shows. For the root domain, `example.com`, a plain CNAME isn't allowed: [RFC 1034](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1034.txt) says that when a CNAME is present at a name, no other data should be, and the root always has NS records. Use the A record the host provides, or a DNS provider that offers a CNAME-like record at the root, such as Cloudflare's [CNAME flattening](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/cname-flattening/) or an ALIAS or ANAME record.

Two mistakes are common. On providers whose Name field expects only the label (`app`), entering the full hostname creates `app.example.com.example.com`. And a retyped target with a typo, or with a trailing period dropped that the host included on purpose, can point somewhere other than the host: paste the value exactly as the host shows it. [Vercel's guide](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/troubleshooting#absolute-cname-records) covers the trailing period under absolute CNAME records.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [3. Remove conflicting records and check what resolvers see](https://www.prisma.io#3-remove-conflicting-records-and-check-what-resolvers-see)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [3. Remove conflicting records and check what resolvers see](https://www.prisma.io#3-remove-conflicting-records-and-check-what-resolvers-see)
payload.content:
## [3. Remove conflicting records and check what resolvers see](https://www.prisma.io#3-remove-conflicting-records-and-check-what-resolvers-see)

Delete old A, AAAA or CNAME records on the same name, such as a registrar's parking page or a previous host. Then check the answer from public resolvers instead of your own machine:

If the answers don't match what the host expects, the problem is still DNS. Resolvers keep an old answer until its TTL expires. [Vercel's guide](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/troubleshooting) recommends lowering the old record's TTL before a switch, and notes that nameserver changes can take up to 24 to 48 hours.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [4. Let the certificate issue, then test HTTPS](https://www.prisma.io#4-let-the-certificate-issue-then-test-https)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [4. Let the certificate issue, then test HTTPS](https://www.prisma.io#4-let-the-certificate-issue-then-test-https)
payload.content:
## [4. Let the certificate issue, then test HTTPS](https://www.prisma.io#4-let-the-certificate-issue-then-test-https)

Most hosts request a certificate for your domain automatically once DNS points at them. With the common [HTTP-01 challenge](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/challenge-types/), the certificate authority fetches a file from your domain, so issuance can't finish until step 3 is done. Check what the server returns:

If HTTP answers and HTTPS fails, the certificate isn't there yet. Two settings often block it:

- **CAA records.** A CAA record lists the certificate authorities allowed to issue for your domain. If you have CAA records, they must allow the authority your host uses. [Let's Encrypt's CAA page](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/caa/) explains the format, and `dig +short CAA example.com` shows yours.
- **A proxy in front of the host.** When Cloudflare proxies a record, lookups return [Cloudflare's addresses](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/proxy-status/) instead of your host's target, so a host that checks the record or serves the HTTP challenge may not see it. Set the record to DNS only, or follow your host's proxy instructions. If you keep the proxy, Cloudflare's Flexible mode sends plain HTTP to the host, and an app that redirects HTTP to HTTPS then [loops](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ssl/troubleshooting/too-many-redirects/). Use Full (strict) once the host has a certificate.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [5. Update the app's own settings](https://www.prisma.io#5-update-the-apps-own-settings)
payload.content:
## [5. Update the app's own settings](https://www.prisma.io#5-update-the-apps-own-settings)

When the domain loads but parts of the app fail, search the code and environment for the generated hostname and change:

- **The base URL.** Environment variables such as `APP_URL` or `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` that build links, redirects and API calls.
- **OAuth redirect URIs.** Identity providers only redirect to URIs registered with them. Google returns `redirect_uri_mismatch` when the URI [doesn't match an authorized redirect URI](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/web-server) for the client. Add the new callback URL in each provider's console.
- **CORS origins.** An API on another hostname must list the new origin in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, and requests with credentials need the exact origin rather than `*` ([MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS)).
- **Cookies.** If the app sets cookies with `Domain` set to the old hostname, browsers [reject them](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie) when the response comes from your domain. Omit `Domain` for a host-only cookie, or set it to your domain.
- **Host checks and redirects.** If your server or framework checks the `Host` header against an allowlist, add the new name. Pick one canonical hostname, for example `www` or the root, and redirect the other to it.

Redeploy after changing environment variables. Many builds read them only when the app builds or starts.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [Custom domains on Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io#custom-domains-on-prisma-compute)
payload.content:
## [Custom domains on Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io#custom-domains-on-prisma-compute)

A [custom domain](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/domains) on Prisma Compute attaches to a production app that has a promoted, running deployment. It uses one CNAME record that points at `switchboard.{region}.prisma.build`, the routing layer in front of the app. Prisma Compute verifies the DNS record, provisions the TLS certificate and terminates TLS, so there is no certificate to upload. The flow runs from the Prisma CLI:

1. Register the domain. Registration checks DNS first, so a run before the record exists fails with `DOMAIN_DNS_NOT_CONFIGURED` and prints the record name and value to create:
2. Create the printed CNAME record at your DNS provider. The CLI prints the full hostname as the record name; enter only the label (`app`) if your provider expects a relative name.
3. Once the record has propagated, run the same `add` command again. TLS provisioning starts, and `wait` polls until the domain is active, for up to 15 minutes:
4. If the domain stays in `pending_dns` or `provisioning_tls`, or ends in `failed`, inspect it, then retry stuck provisioning:

`show` prints the state, certificate details and any DNS hints. `retry` returns `DOMAIN_RETRY_NOT_ELIGIBLE` when the domain isn't in a retryable state.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [Custom domains on Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io#custom-domains-on-prisma-compute)
payload.content:
`show` prints the state, certificate details and any DNS hints. `retry` returns `DOMAIN_RETRY_NOT_ELIGIBLE` when the domain isn't in a retryable state.

The record has to resolve to the Switchboard target. The [launch post on custom domains](https://www.prisma.io/blog/prisma-compute-custom-domains) says validation accepts "either the expected CNAME target or the underlying regional records associated with that target." A record proxied through Cloudflare answers with [Cloudflare's anycast addresses](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/proxy-status/) instead, so if you use Cloudflare DNS, set the record to DNS only (gray cloud). Keeping the proxy, the other option in step 4, isn't documented for Prisma Compute.

Steps 3 and 5 of the general fix still apply, as does the CAA check in step 4: remove conflicting records, keep CAA records compatible with certificate issuance, and give the app's base URL, OAuth callbacks and cookies the new name. Environment variable values on Prisma Compute resolve at deploy time, so deploy again after you change them. Prisma Compute doesn't require Prisma ORM or Prisma Postgres, so this applies to any app you deploy there.

The limits on the [Domains page](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/domains) and [Known limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations) decide whether this setup fits:

- Custom domains attach to production apps only. Preview apps keep their generated URLs.
- DNS uses CNAME records only. A root domain needs a DNS provider with ALIAS, ANAME or CNAME flattening. Without one, put the app on a subdomain such as `www` or `app`.
- Wildcard hostnames such as `*.example.com` are rejected.
- Each service can have up to 3 custom domains.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [How to prevent it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it)
payload.content:
## [How to prevent it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it)

Lower the TTL on the existing record a day before you switch hosts, so a mistake rolls back quickly. Keep the generated URL working: it is the control that tells you whether a failure is in the app or in the domain setup. Keep the canonical URL in one environment variable rather than in code, and register OAuth callbacks for every hostname you serve before you move traffic.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [When this fix doesn't apply](https://www.prisma.io#when-this-fix-doesnt-apply)
payload.content:
## [When this fix doesn't apply](https://www.prisma.io#when-this-fix-doesnt-apply)

If the generated URL fails too, the problem is in the app or the deployment, not the domain. Check the deploy logs first. If the domain works for you but not for some visitors, compare resolvers and networks before changing records, because a cached answer or a network that filters traffic can explain it.

Some setups need a feature a host may not offer: a wildcard domain for many tenants, a custom domain on a preview environment, or an A record at the root because your DNS provider has no CNAME flattening. Prisma Compute supports none of these today, as [the Domains page](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/domains) lists, so choose a host that does if you need one of them.

payload.content:

`dig @1.1.1.1 app.example.com` to see what the internet sees, rather than relying on your own browser, which may have cached the old result.`www` or `app` takes a normal CNAME.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: What hosting should I use for customer reports?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports?
payload.content:
## What hosting should I use for customer reports?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute),

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)and an Object Store bucket keep those resources in one project. That is a practical fit for a TypeScript business app with bounded report requests. Keep Vercel or Netlify when their existing workflow fits, and choose a suitable worker runtime for generation that must finish independently of a request.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)6 min read

The report is useful only if the right customer can obtain the right result. That includes a saved filter choice, a defined view of the data, a generation status and a file that still exists after the next deployment.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The linked hosting, storage and PostgreSQL documentation was checked on October 22, 2026.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [What determines the hosting setup?](https://www.prisma.io#what-determines-the-hosting-setup)
payload.content:
## [What determines the hosting setup?](https://www.prisma.io#what-determines-the-hosting-setup)

Start with the actual report engine and workload. A small CSV can come from a bounded database query. A large PDF may need a rendering library, substantial memory or a browser process. Test that dependency in the intended runtime before choosing a host.

Decide whether the result must be generated during the request or can arrive later. Measure query time, rendering time, output size and concurrent requests with a representative dataset. A successful two-row demo does not establish how a customer's largest report behaves.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [Which app host fits the report endpoint?](https://www.prisma.io#which-app-host-fits-the-report-endpoint)
payload.content:
## [Which app host fits the report endpoint?](https://www.prisma.io#which-app-host-fits-the-report-endpoint)

These app hosts are listed alphabetically. Each can connect to managed Postgres and an appropriate object store.

| Setup | Useful fit | Verify before launch | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify + Prisma Postgres | An existing app built around [Netlify functions](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/overview/). | The chosen runtime supports the renderer and the report fits the function's documented limits. | 
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres + Object Store | A TypeScript app that wants its server, database and [private files](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/object-storage) in one project. | The deployed Bun runtime supports the report engine, and longer work has a durable execution plan. | 
| Vercel + Prisma Postgres | A Next.js app already using [Vercel functions](https://vercel.com/docs/functions). | Renderer dependencies, request duration and how unfinished work is recovered. | 

For a new TypeScript app serving small customer-scoped reports, Compute keeps the endpoint and saved data together. You can also use Prisma Postgres while keeping the report API on an existing host.

payload.section: [1. Define the report and its customer boundary](https://www.prisma.io#1-define-the-report-and-its-customer-boundary)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [1. Define the report and its customer boundary](https://www.prisma.io#1-define-the-report-and-its-customer-boundary)
payload.content:
## [1. Define the report and its customer boundary](https://www.prisma.io#1-define-the-report-and-its-customer-boundary)

Create a development Prisma Postgres database and a private [Object Store bucket](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/object-storage) in the intended project. Use fictional customer data and separate storage from production while testing.

Store a report identifier, owning account, requested filters, generation state, creation time and eventual object key. The server derives the account from verified authentication. A request's account field or an unguessable report identifier is not sufficient permission to query or download another customer's data.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [2. Check the query before adding a renderer](https://www.prisma.io#2-check-the-query-before-adding-a-renderer)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [2. Check the query before adding a renderer](https://www.prisma.io#2-check-the-query-before-adding-a-renderer)
payload.content:
## [2. Check the query before adding a renderer](https://www.prisma.io#2-check-the-query-before-adding-a-renderer)

With `psql` installed, open a development database connection and run this self-contained example. It reads fictional values and creates no tables:

The result is `order_count = 2` and `total_cents = 17500`. The other account is excluded. In application code, bind the authorized account as a parameter and validate report filters. The constant in this demonstration is not an authentication implementation.

Define whether a report describes current data or a saved state at a particular time. For a small report that needs several queries to agree, begin a short read-only transaction at PostgreSQL's [Repeatable Read isolation level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html#XACT-REPEATABLE-READ) before the first query. Collect the authorized inputs and commit before rendering or uploading. For large exports, design a saved or versioned input dataset rather than holding an open transaction through a long rendering job. Pagination alone does not freeze records that are being updated.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [3. Choose synchronous or queued generation](https://www.prisma.io#3-choose-synchronous-or-queued-generation)
payload.content:
## [3. Choose synchronous or queued generation](https://www.prisma.io#3-choose-synchronous-or-queued-generation)

For a bounded report, query authorized data, render it and return the result within the host's limits. Handle client disconnects and errors without reporting a completed download that never existed.

Compute has [60 seconds to start responding](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout). Streaming can continue after the first response bytes, but it does not make a generation task durable. If work must finish independently of the request, save a report job and give it a deployed worker with a reliable trigger, retry policy and recovery after interruption.

The [Postgres job-queue guide](https://www.prisma.io/blog/you-dont-need-a-job-queue-postgres-already-has-skip-locked#where-to-run-the-worker) covers worker hosting. A process that must poll while there are no visitors belongs on a suitable always-on worker host. `waitUntil` can keep a Compute instance awake for best-effort work, but it does not supply durable retries or survive every redeploy.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [4. Publish the file only after it exists](https://www.prisma.io#4-publish-the-file-only-after-it-exists)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [4. Publish the file only after it exists](https://www.prisma.io#4-publish-the-file-only-after-it-exists)
payload.content:
## [4. Publish the file only after it exists](https://www.prisma.io#4-publish-the-file-only-after-it-exists)

Upload the finished result to a private object key for that job attempt, then mark the report ready in Postgres with that reference. An object upload and a database transaction are separate operations. If the state update fails, retry or reconcile the saved job and object; clean up abandoned attempt files through a defined procedure.

Before issuing a download, check that the authenticated account owns the ready report. The [object storage guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/object-storage) shows presigned URLs; set a short lifetime and keep the bucket private, with credentials available only to the server.

When generating CSV from customer-entered text, handle both CSV quoting and spreadsheet interpretation of formulas. Follow [CSV injection guidance](https://community.owasp.org/attacks/CSV_Injection) for values that spreadsheet software may execute; quoting a cell does not by itself make it inert.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [5. Deploy and test recovery](https://www.prisma.io#5-deploy-and-test-recovery)
payload.content:
## [5. Deploy and test recovery](https://www.prisma.io#5-deploy-and-test-recovery)

Configure the server with [Compute getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started) or [Port an existing app](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/porting-an-app). Build before deploying and prepare each database with its [migrations](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/production-database-migrations). A newly declared deployment database does not inherit the Console development database's records.

Test a large report, two accounts requesting the same type, a failed upload, a worker restart and a repeated generation request. Verify that an unauthorized account cannot obtain the report and that the ready file survives an app redeploy. Put report progress and failure information in an authenticated status view.

payload.title: Prisma ORM

payload.content:
## [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)

Choose a worker runtime that supports the renderer when it needs dependencies outside [Compute's runtime limits](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations), or when generation must run as an always-on process. Compute can remain the customer-facing app while the worker uses the same managed Postgres database.

For internal analysis, an existing reporting or BI product may be more appropriate than a custom download service. For saved business data, choose the [backup and restore plan](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) separately from file delivery; a downloadable report is not a backup of the underlying database.

payload.content:
## Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)is a good fit for a TypeScript handoff because its CLI exposes services, live versions and logs, with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)available in the same project. Netlify and Vercel also expose deployment details. A successful build is one check; sign-in, database writes and the correct live version need their own checks.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)7 min read

A handoff should leave the owner able to answer three questions: which version is live, whether its server can do the business task, and where to look when that task fails. The contractor's working laptop and a green build indicator do not answer all three.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. Provider sources linked here were checked on October 19, 2026. The service commands below inspect existing resources without deploying code or changing configuration. The acceptance test in step 3 writes a fictional record in production; use an agreed test account and clean up afterward.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [What evidence should the owner be able to see?](https://www.prisma.io#what-evidence-should-the-owner-be-able-to-see)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [What evidence should the owner be able to see?](https://www.prisma.io#what-evidence-should-the-owner-be-able-to-see)
payload.content:
## [What evidence should the owner be able to see?](https://www.prisma.io#what-evidence-should-the-owner-be-able-to-see)

Ask for the repository commit, platform project, production URL and service or deployment identifier. Keep the hosting account, domain and database ownership with the business. Give the contractor the platform access their work needs, then review access at handoff.

Separate build output from runtime evidence. Build logs explain compilation and packaging; runtime logs explain requests to the running server. Neither proves by itself that a customer can log in and save the right record. Agree on an acceptance test that covers the workflow the business bought.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [Which host exposes useful deployment evidence?](https://www.prisma.io#which-host-exposes-useful-deployment-evidence)
payload.content:
## [Which host exposes useful deployment evidence?](https://www.prisma.io#which-host-exposes-useful-deployment-evidence)

These hosts are listed alphabetically. Each needs an application-level acceptance test.

| Host | What the owner can inspect | When it fits | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify | [Deploy summaries and deploy logs](https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/deploy-overview/), plus [function logs](https://docs.netlify.com/manage/monitoring/logs/). | The app already uses Netlify's framework and function workflow. | 
| Prisma Compute | [Service details, live versions and version logs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/service); build output is available in Console. | You want TypeScript hosting and managed Postgres in one project, with CLI inspection for the owner or their assistant. | 
| Vercel | [Deployment details and build output](https://vercel.com/docs/deployments), plus [runtime logs](https://vercel.com/docs/logs). | The Next.js app already follows Vercel's deployment workflow. | 

Keep an existing host if it already gives the owner the access and evidence they need. Prisma Postgres can remain the database from another app host; moving the frontend is optional.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [1. Confirm the account, project and service](https://www.prisma.io#1-confirm-the-account-project-and-service)
payload.content:
## [1. Confirm the account, project and service](https://www.prisma.io#1-confirm-the-account-project-and-service)

Use a supported CLI runtime from the [getting-started guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started). The commands use `prisma@latest` so an older project-local CLI is not selected. The current Prisma 8 CLI is a [release candidate](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/release-status); inspecting hosting resources does not require upgrading the app's ORM.

Authenticate as the intended account, then inspect an existing project named `customer-portal`. Here `main` is the project's confirmed production branch; replace it if your project uses another branch:

Use the service name actually returned by the list. The next commands assume it is `web` and keep the same explicit branch so a similarly named preview does not confuse the handoff:

The [service reference](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/service) describes these outputs. `service show` identifies the live version; the version list gives history. Keep that identifier with the agreed source commit and deployment report. The commands show real account-specific values, so there is no universal successful output to paste into a checklist.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [2. Check the intended URL and version](https://www.prisma.io#2-check-the-intended-url-and-version)
payload.content:
## [2. Check the intended URL and version](https://www.prisma.io#2-check-the-intended-url-and-version)

Open the live service URL from its details, then the production custom domain if one is configured. Verify the expected release marker or feature and compare it with the handoff's commit and version record. A preview can work while a production domain still serves an earlier release.

For a deployment created by an assistant or CI, retain the [deploy report](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/deploy) with its resource results and URLs. Verify its outcome and the actual live version. A process starting successfully is not the same as a completed acceptance test.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [3. Run an authenticated business action](https://www.prisma.io#3-run-an-authenticated-business-action)
payload.content:
## [3. Run an authenticated business action](https://www.prisma.io#3-run-an-authenticated-business-action)

This test writes to production through the live URL. Use the agreed test account to sign in, create or update a fictional record, reload the page and confirm the saved state. Verify that an unauthorized account cannot read it. Clean up the fictional record afterward through the application's normal workflow.

For Prisma Postgres, confirm the resource the app actually connects to and that its migrations are applied. A service can deploy while pointing to an empty test database or to credentials for the wrong environment. [Secret scopes](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-app-secrets) and database identity belong in the handoff notes without recording secret values.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [4. Check failures and the recovery path](https://www.prisma.io#4-check-failures-and-the-recovery-path)
payload.content:
## [4. Check failures and the recovery path](https://www.prisma.io#4-check-failures-and-the-recovery-path)

Read runtime logs around the acceptance request. `service logs` defaults to the live version; use `--version-id` when investigating an older one. If runtime logs are unavailable for that version, retain its ID and consult Console build output or application monitoring. Avoid writing passwords, tokens or customer payloads to logs.

Agree who handles failed deploys and how to use the [rollback procedure](https://www.prisma.io/compute/roll-back-deployment). Test recovery on a review environment and check schema compatibility. Also confirm that billing, backups and the domain can be managed by someone the business retains.

When the business operates several independent apps, keep the handoff record per app. The [multiple-app hosting guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/multiple-business-apps) covers separate projects, databases, credentials and release boundaries under shared administration.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)
payload.content:
## [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)

Choose the host whose runtime and operating workflow fit the app. Prisma Compute runs deployed services on Bun and currently lacks WebSocket server support and a persistent writable filesystem. Check the [runtime limits](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations) before accepting dependencies that require those features.

If the owner requires a particular monitoring integration or log retention period, verify that separately. A short deploy log and a permanent application audit record serve different needs, and the handoff should state where each lives.

After accepting the release, keep an [owner operations record](https://www.prisma.io/compute/business-app-operations) with routine checks, recovery steps and a route to technical help.
