payload.content:
## DataFrame creation[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#dataframe-creation)

Similar to the previous section where a single column was converted to categorical, all columns in a
`DataFrame` can be batch converted to categorical either during or after construction.

This can be done during construction by specifying `dtype="category"` in the `DataFrame` constructor:

```
In [17]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": list("abca"), "B": list("bccd")}, dtype="category")
In [18]: df.dtypes
Out[18]: 
A    category
B    category
dtype: object
```
Note that the categories present in each column differ; the conversion is done column by column, so only labels present in a given column are categories:

```
In [19]: df["A"]
Out[19]: 
0    a
1    b
2    c
3    a
Name: A, dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
In [20]: df["B"]
Out[20]: 
0    b
1    c
2    c
3    d
Name: B, dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['b', 'c', 'd']
```
Analogously, all columns in an existing `DataFrame` can be batch converted using [`DataFrame.astype()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.astype.html#pandas.DataFrame.astype):

```
In [21]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": list("abca"), "B": list("bccd")})
In [22]: df_cat = df.astype("category")
In [23]: df_cat.dtypes
Out[23]: 
A    category
B    category
dtype: object
```
This conversion is likewise done column by column:

```
In [24]: df_cat["A"]
Out[24]: 
0    a
1    b
2    c
3    a
Name: A, dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
In [25]: df_cat["B"]
Out[25]: 
0    b
1    c
2    c
3    d
Name: B, dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['b', 'c', 'd']
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Categorical data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categorical-data) > Controlling behavior[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#controlling-behavior)
payload.content:
## Controlling behavior[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#controlling-behavior)

In the examples above where we passed `dtype='category'`, we used the default
behavior:

1. Categories are inferred from the data.
2. Categories are unordered.

To control those behaviors, instead of passing `'category'`, use an instance
of `CategoricalDtype`.

```
In [26]: from pandas.api.types import CategoricalDtype
In [27]: s = pd.Series([None, "b", "c", None])
In [28]: cat_type = CategoricalDtype(categories=["b", "c", "d"], ordered=True)
In [29]: s_cat = s.astype(cat_type)
In [30]: s_cat
Out[30]: 
0    NaN
1      b
2      c
3    NaN
dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['b' < 'c' < 'd']
```
Similarly, a `CategoricalDtype` can be used with a `DataFrame` to ensure that categories
are consistent among all columns.

```
In [31]: from pandas.api.types import CategoricalDtype
In [32]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": list("abca"), "B": list("bccd")})
In [33]: cat_type = CategoricalDtype(categories=list("abcd"), ordered=True)
In [34]: df_cat = df.astype(cat_type)
In [35]: df_cat["A"]
Out[35]: 
0    a
1    b
2    c
3    a
Name: A, dtype: category
Categories (4, str): ['a' < 'b' < 'c' < 'd']
In [36]: df_cat["B"]
Out[36]: 
0    b
1    c
2    c
3    d
Name: B, dtype: category
Categories (4, str): ['a' < 'b' < 'c' < 'd']
```
Note

To perform table-wise conversion, where all labels in the entire `DataFrame` are used as
categories for each column, the `categories` parameter can be determined programmatically by
`categories = pd.unique(df.to_numpy().ravel())`.

If you already have `codes` and `categories`, you can use the
[`from_codes()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.from_codes.html#pandas.Categorical.from_codes) constructor to save the factorize step
during normal constructor mode:

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Categorical data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categorical-data) > Controlling behavior[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#controlling-behavior)
payload.content:
[`from_codes()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.from_codes.html#pandas.Categorical.from_codes) constructor to save the factorize step
during normal constructor mode:

```
In [37]: splitter = np.random.choice([0, 1], 5, p=[0.5, 0.5])
In [38]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical.from_codes(splitter, categories=["train", "test"]))
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Categorical data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categorical-data) > Regaining original data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#regaining-original-data)
payload.content:
## Regaining original data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#regaining-original-data)

To get back to the original `Series` or NumPy array, use
`Series.astype(original_dtype)` or `np.asarray(categorical)`:

```
In [39]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"])
In [40]: s
Out[40]: 
0    a
1    b
2    c
3    a
dtype: str
In [41]: s2 = s.astype("category")
In [42]: s2
Out[42]: 
0    a
1    b
2    c
3    a
dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
In [43]: s2.astype(str)
Out[43]: 
0    a
1    b
2    c
3    a
dtype: str
In [44]: np.asarray(s2)
Out[44]: array(['a', 'b', 'c', 'a'], dtype=object)
```
Note

In contrast to R’s `factor` function, categorical data is not converting input values to
strings; categories will end up the same data type as the original values.

Note

In contrast to R’s `factor` function, there is currently no way to assign/change labels at
creation time. Use `categories` to change the categories after creation time.

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Categorical data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categorical-data) > CategoricalDtype[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categoricaldtype)
payload.content:
## CategoricalDtype[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categoricaldtype)

A categorical’s type is fully described by

1. `categories`: a sequence of unique values and no missing values
2. `ordered`: a boolean

This information can be stored in a `CategoricalDtype`.
The `categories` argument is optional, which implies that the actual categories
should be inferred from whatever is present in the data when the
[`pandas.Categorical`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.html#pandas.Categorical) is created. The categories are assumed to be unordered
by default.

```
In [45]: from pandas.api.types import CategoricalDtype
In [46]: CategoricalDtype(["a", "b", "c"])
Out[46]: CategoricalDtype(categories=['a', 'b', 'c'], ordered=False, categories_dtype=str)
In [47]: CategoricalDtype(["a", "b", "c"], ordered=True)
Out[47]: CategoricalDtype(categories=['a', 'b', 'c'], ordered=True, categories_dtype=str)
In [48]: CategoricalDtype()
Out[48]: CategoricalDtype(categories=None, ordered=False, categories_dtype=None)
```
A `CategoricalDtype` can be used in any place pandas
expects a `dtype`. For example [`pandas.read_csv()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html#pandas.read_csv),
[`pandas.DataFrame.astype()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.astype.html#pandas.DataFrame.astype), or in the `Series` constructor.

Note

As a convenience, you can use the string `'category'` in place of a
`CategoricalDtype` when you want the default behavior of
the categories being unordered, and equal to the set values present in the
array. In other words, `dtype='category'` is equivalent to
`dtype=CategoricalDtype()`.

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Categorical data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categorical-data) > Equality semantics[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#equality-semantics)
payload.content:
## Equality semantics[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#equality-semantics)

Two instances of `CategoricalDtype` compare equal
whenever they have the same categories and order. When comparing two
unordered categoricals, the order of the `categories` is not considered. Note
that categories with different dtypes are not the same.

```
In [49]: c1 = CategoricalDtype(["a", "b", "c"], ordered=False)

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.section: Equal, since order is not considered when ordered=False
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Equal, since order is not considered when ordered=False
payload.content:
## Equal, since order is not considered when ordered=False

In [50]: c1 == CategoricalDtype(["b", "c", "a"], ordered=False)
Out[50]: True

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.section: Unequal, since the second CategoricalDtype is ordered
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Unequal, since the second CategoricalDtype is ordered
payload.content:
## Unequal, since the second CategoricalDtype is ordered

In [51]: c1 == CategoricalDtype(["a", "b", "c"], ordered=True)
Out[51]: False
```
All instances of `CategoricalDtype` compare equal to the string `'category'`.

```
In [52]: c1 == "category"
Out[52]: True
```
Notice that the `categories_dtype` should be considered, especially when comparing with
two empty `CategoricalDtype` instances.

```
In [53]: c2 = pd.Categorical(np.array([], dtype=object))
In [54]: c3 = pd.Categorical(np.array([], dtype=float))
In [55]: c2.dtype == c3.dtype
Out[55]: False
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Unequal, since the second CategoricalDtype is ordered > Description[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#description)
payload.content:
## Description[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#description)

Using [`describe()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.describe.html#pandas.DataFrame.describe) on categorical data will produce similar
output to a `Series` or `DataFrame` of type `string`.

```
In [56]: cat = pd.Categorical(["a", "c", "c", np.nan], categories=["b", "a", "c"])
In [57]: df = pd.DataFrame({"cat": cat, "s": ["a", "c", "c", np.nan]})
In [58]: df.describe()
Out[58]: 
       cat  s
count    3  3
unique   2  2
top      c  c
freq     2  2
In [59]: df["cat"].describe()
Out[59]: 
count     3
unique    2
top       c
freq      2
Name: cat, dtype: object
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Unequal, since the second CategoricalDtype is ordered > Working with categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#working-with-categories)
payload.content:
## Working with categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#working-with-categories)

Categorical data has a `categories` and a `ordered` property, which list their
possible values and whether the ordering matters or not. These properties are
exposed as `s.cat.categories` and `s.cat.ordered`. If you don’t manually
specify categories and ordering, they are inferred from the passed arguments.

```
In [60]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"], dtype="category")
In [61]: s.cat.categories
Out[61]: Index(['a', 'b', 'c'], dtype='str')
In [62]: s.cat.ordered
Out[62]: False
```
It’s also possible to pass in the categories in a specific order:

```
In [63]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "c", "a"], categories=["c", "b", "a"]))
In [64]: s.cat.categories
Out[64]: Index(['c', 'b', 'a'], dtype='str')
In [65]: s.cat.ordered
Out[65]: False
```
Note

New categorical data are **not** automatically ordered. You must explicitly
pass `ordered=True` to indicate an ordered `Categorical`.

Note

The result of [`unique()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.unique.html#pandas.Series.unique) is not always the same as `Series.cat.categories`,
because `Series.unique()` has a couple of guarantees, namely that it returns categories
in the order of appearance, and it only includes values that are actually present.

```
In [66]: s = pd.Series(list("babc")).astype(CategoricalDtype(list("abcd")))
In [67]: s
Out[67]: 
0    b
1    a
2    b
3    c
dtype: category
Categories (4, str): ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > categories
payload.content:
## categories

In [68]: s.cat.categories
Out[68]: Index(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'], dtype='str')

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > uniques
payload.content:
## uniques

In [69]: s.unique()
Out[69]: 
['b', 'a', 'c']
Categories (4, str): ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > uniques > Renaming categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#renaming-categories)
payload.content:
## Renaming categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#renaming-categories)

Renaming categories is done by using the
[`rename_categories()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.rename_categories.html#pandas.Categorical.rename_categories) method:

```
In [70]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"], dtype="category")
In [71]: s
Out[71]: 
0    a
1    b
2    c
3    a
dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
In [72]: new_categories = ["Group %s" % g for g in s.cat.categories]
In [73]: s = s.cat.rename_categories(new_categories)
In [74]: s
Out[74]: 
0    Group a
1    Group b
2    Group c
3    Group a
dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['Group a', 'Group b', 'Group c']

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.section: You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming
payload.content:
## You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming

In [75]: s = s.cat.rename_categories({"Group a": "x", "Group b": "y", "Group c": "z"})
In [76]: s
Out[76]: 
0    x
1    y
2    z
3    x
dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['x', 'y', 'z']
```
Note

In contrast to R’s `factor`, categorical data can have categories of other types than string.

Categories must be unique or a `ValueError` is raised:

```
In [77]: try:
   ....:     s = s.cat.rename_categories([1, 1, 1])
   ....: except ValueError as e:
   ....:     print("ValueError:", str(e))
   ....: 
ValueError: Categorical categories must be unique
```
Categories must also not be `NaN` or a `ValueError` is raised:

```
In [78]: try:
   ....:     s = s.cat.rename_categories([1, 2, np.nan])
   ....: except ValueError as e:
   ....:     print("ValueError:", str(e))
   ....: 
ValueError: Categorical categories cannot be null
```
To merge several categories into one, use [`Series.replace()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.replace.html#pandas.Series.replace) to replace the
values and then drop the categories that are no longer used with
[`remove_unused_categories()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.cat.remove_unused_categories.html#pandas.Series.cat.remove_unused_categories):

```
In [79]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"], dtype="category")
In [80]: s = s.replace({"a": "b"}).cat.remove_unused_categories()
In [81]: s
Out[81]: 
0    b
1    b
2    c
3    b
dtype: category
Categories (2, str): ['b', 'c']
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming > Appending new categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#appending-new-categories)
payload.content:
## Appending new categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#appending-new-categories)

Appending categories can be done by using the
[`add_categories()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.add_categories.html#pandas.Categorical.add_categories) method:

```
In [82]: s = s.cat.add_categories([4])
In [83]: s.cat.categories
Out[83]: Index(['b', 'c', 4], dtype='object')
In [84]: s
Out[84]: 
0    b
1    b
2    c
3    b
dtype: category
Categories (3, object): ['b', 'c', 4]
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming > Removing categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#removing-categories)
payload.content:
## Removing categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#removing-categories)

Removing categories can be done by using the
[`remove_categories()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.remove_categories.html#pandas.Categorical.remove_categories) method. Values which are removed
are replaced by `np.nan`.:

```
In [85]: s = s.cat.remove_categories([4])
In [86]: s
Out[86]: 
0    b
1    b
2    c
3    b
dtype: category
Categories (2, object): ['b', 'c']
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming > Removing unused categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#removing-unused-categories)
payload.content:
## Removing unused categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#removing-unused-categories)

Removing unused categories can also be done:

```
In [87]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "a"], categories=["a", "b", "c", "d"]))
In [88]: s
Out[88]: 
0    a
1    b
2    a
dtype: category
Categories (4, str): ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']
In [89]: s.cat.remove_unused_categories()
Out[89]: 
0    a
1    b
2    a
dtype: category
Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming > Setting categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#setting-categories)
payload.content:
## Setting categories[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#setting-categories)

If you want to do remove and add new categories in one step (which has some
speed advantage), or simply set the categories to a predefined scale,
use [`set_categories()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.set_categories.html#pandas.Categorical.set_categories).

```
In [90]: s = pd.Series(["one", "two", "four", "-"], dtype="category")
In [91]: s
Out[91]: 
0     one
1     two
2    four
3       -
dtype: category
Categories (4, str): ['-', 'four', 'one', 'two']
In [92]: s = s.cat.set_categories(["one", "two", "three", "four"])
In [93]: s
Out[93]: 
0     one
1     two
2    four
3     NaN
dtype: category
Categories (4, str): ['one', 'two', 'three', 'four']
```
Note

Be aware that [`Categorical.set_categories()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.set_categories.html#pandas.Categorical.set_categories) cannot know whether some category is omitted
intentionally or because it is misspelled or (under Python3) due to a type difference (e.g.,
NumPy S1 dtype and Python strings). This can result in surprising behaviour!

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming > Sorting and order[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#sorting-and-order)
payload.content:
## Sorting and order[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#sorting-and-order)

If categorical data is ordered (`s.cat.ordered == True`), then the order of the categories has a
meaning and certain operations are possible. If the categorical is unordered, `.min()/.max()` will raise a `TypeError`.

```
In [94]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "c", "a"], ordered=False))
In [95]: s = s.sort_values()
In [96]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"]).astype(CategoricalDtype(ordered=True))
In [97]: s = s.sort_values()
In [98]: s
Out[98]: 
0    a
3    a
1    b
2    c
dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a' < 'b' < 'c']
In [99]: s.min(), s.max()
Out[99]: ('a', 'c')
```
You can set categorical data to be ordered by using `as_ordered()` or unordered by using `as_unordered()`. These will by
default return a *new* object.

```
In [100]: s.cat.as_ordered()
Out[100]: 
0    a
3    a
1    b
2    c
dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a' < 'b' < 'c']
In [101]: s.cat.as_unordered()
Out[101]: 
0    a
3    a
1    b
2    c
dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
```
Sorting will use the order defined by categories, not any lexical order present on the data type. This is even true for strings and numeric data:

```
In [102]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 1], dtype="category")
In [103]: s = s.cat.set_categories([2, 3, 1], ordered=True)
In [104]: s
Out[104]: 
0    1
1    2
2    3
3    1
dtype: category
Categories (3, int64): [2 < 3 < 1]
In [105]: s = s.sort_values()
In [106]: s
Out[106]: 
1    2
2    3
0    1
3    1
dtype: category
Categories (3, int64): [2 < 3 < 1]
In [107]: s.min(), s.max()
Out[107]: (np.int64(2), np.int64(1))
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming > Reordering[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#reordering)
payload.content:
## Reordering[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#reordering)

Reordering the categories is possible via the [`Categorical.reorder_categories()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.reorder_categories.html#pandas.Categorical.reorder_categories) and
the [`Categorical.set_categories()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.set_categories.html#pandas.Categorical.set_categories) methods. For [`Categorical.reorder_categories()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Categorical.reorder_categories.html#pandas.Categorical.reorder_categories), all
old categories must be included in the new categories and no new categories are allowed. This will
necessarily make the sort order the same as the categories order.

```
In [108]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 1], dtype="category")
In [109]: s = s.cat.reorder_categories([2, 3, 1], ordered=True)
In [110]: s
Out[110]: 
0    1
1    2
2    3
3    1
dtype: category
Categories (3, int64): [2 < 3 < 1]
In [111]: s = s.sort_values()
In [112]: s
Out[112]: 
1    2
2    3
0    1
3    1
dtype: category
Categories (3, int64): [2 < 3 < 1]
In [113]: s.min(), s.max()
Out[113]: (np.int64(2), np.int64(1))
```
Note

Note the difference between assigning new categories and reordering the categories: the first
renames categories and therefore the individual values in the `Series`, but if the first
position was sorted last, the renamed value will still be sorted last. Reordering means that the
way values are sorted is different afterwards, but not that individual values in the
`Series` are changed.

Note

payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming > Reordering[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#reordering)
payload.content:
position was sorted last, the renamed value will still be sorted last. Reordering means that the
way values are sorted is different afterwards, but not that individual values in the
`Series` are changed.

Note

If the `Categorical` is not ordered, [`Series.min()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.min.html#pandas.Series.min) and [`Series.max()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.max.html#pandas.Series.max) will raise
`TypeError`. Numeric operations like `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and operations based on them
(e.g. [`Series.median()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.median.html#pandas.Series.median), which would need to compute the mean between two values if the length
of an array is even) do not work and raise a `TypeError`.

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming > Multi column sorting[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#multi-column-sorting)
payload.content:
## Multi column sorting[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#multi-column-sorting)

A categorical dtyped column will participate in a multi-column sort in a similar manner to other columns.
The ordering of the categorical is determined by the `categories` of that column.

```
In [114]: dfs = pd.DataFrame(
   .....:     {
   .....:         "A": pd.Categorical(
   .....:             list("bbeebbaa"),
   .....:             categories=["e", "a", "b"],
   .....:             ordered=True,
   .....:         ),
   .....:         "B": [1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1],
   .....:     }
   .....: )
   .....: 
In [115]: dfs.sort_values(by=["A", "B"])
Out[115]: 
   A  B
2  e  1
3  e  2
7  a  1
6  a  2
0  b  1
5  b  1
1  b  2
4  b  2
```
Reordering the `categories` changes a future sort.

```
In [116]: dfs["A"] = dfs["A"].cat.reorder_categories(["a", "b", "e"])
In [117]: dfs.sort_values(by=["A", "B"])
Out[117]: 
   A  B
7  a  1
6  a  2
0  b  1
5  b  1
1  b  2
4  b  2
2  e  1
3  e  2
```

payload.content:
## Comparisons[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#comparisons)

Comparing categorical data with other objects is possible in three cases:

- Comparing equality (`==` and `!=`) to a list-like object (list, Series, array,
…) of the same length as the categorical data.
- All comparisons (`==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, and `<=`) of categorical data to
another categorical Series, when `ordered==True` and the `categories` are the same.
- All comparisons of a categorical data to a scalar.

All other comparisons, especially “non-equality” comparisons of two categoricals with different
categories or a categorical with any list-like object, will raise a `TypeError`.

Note

Any “non-equality” comparisons of categorical data with a `Series`, `np.array`, `list` or
categorical data with different categories or ordering will raise a `TypeError` because custom
categories ordering could be interpreted in two ways: one with taking into account the
ordering and one without.

```
In [118]: cat = pd.Series([1, 2, 3]).astype(CategoricalDtype([3, 2, 1], ordered=True))
In [119]: cat_base = pd.Series([2, 2, 2]).astype(CategoricalDtype([3, 2, 1], ordered=True))
In [120]: cat_base2 = pd.Series([2, 2, 2]).astype(CategoricalDtype(ordered=True))
In [121]: cat
Out[121]: 
0    1
1    2
2    3
dtype: category
Categories (3, int64): [3 < 2 < 1]
In [122]: cat_base
Out[122]: 
0    2
1    2
2    2
dtype: category
Categories (3, int64): [3 < 2 < 1]
In [123]: cat_base2
Out[123]: 
0    2
1    2
2    2
dtype: category
Categories (1, int64): [2]
```
Comparing to a categorical with the same categories and ordering or to a scalar works:

```
In [124]: cat > cat_base
Out[124]: 
0     True
1    False
2    False
dtype: bool
In [125]: cat > 2
Out[125]: 
0     True
1    False
2    False
dtype: bool
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming > Comparisons[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#comparisons)
payload.content:
Comparing to a categorical with the same categories and ordering or to a scalar works:

```
In [124]: cat > cat_base
Out[124]: 
0     True
1    False
2    False
dtype: bool
In [125]: cat > 2
Out[125]: 
0     True
1    False
2    False
dtype: bool
```
Equality comparisons work with any list-like object of same length and scalars:

```
In [126]: cat == cat_base
Out[126]: 
0    False
1     True
2    False
dtype: bool
In [127]: cat == np.array([1, 2, 3])
Out[127]: 
0    True
1    True
2    True
dtype: bool
In [128]: cat == 2
Out[128]: 
0    False
1     True
2    False
dtype: bool
```
This doesn’t work because the categories are not the same:

```
In [129]: try:
   .....:     cat > cat_base2
   .....: except TypeError as e:
   .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
   .....: 
TypeError: Categoricals can only be compared if 'categories' are the same.
```
If you want to do a “non-equality” comparison of a categorical series with a list-like object which is not categorical data, you need to be explicit and convert the categorical data back to the original values:

```
In [130]: base = np.array([1, 2, 3])
In [131]: try:
   .....:     cat > base
   .....: except TypeError as e:
   .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
   .....: 
TypeError: Cannot compare a Categorical for op __gt__ with type <class 'numpy.ndarray'>.
If you want to compare values, use 'np.asarray(cat) <op> other'.
In [132]: np.asarray(cat) > base
Out[132]: array([False, False, False])
```
When you compare two unordered categoricals with the same categories, the order is not considered:

```
In [133]: c1 = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"], categories=["a", "b"], ordered=False)
In [134]: c2 = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"], categories=["b", "a"], ordered=False)
In [135]: c1 == c2
Out[135]: array([ True,  True])
```

payload.content:
## Operations[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#operations)

Apart from [`Series.min()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.min.html#pandas.Series.min), [`Series.max()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.max.html#pandas.Series.max) and [`Series.mode()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.mode.html#pandas.Series.mode), the
following operations are possible with categorical data:

`Series` methods like [`Series.value_counts()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.value_counts.html#pandas.Series.value_counts) will use all categories,
even if some categories are not present in the data:

```
In [136]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "c", "c"], categories=["c", "a", "b", "d"]))
In [137]: s.value_counts()
Out[137]: 
c    2
a    1
b    1
d    0
Name: count, dtype: int64
```
`DataFrame` methods like [`DataFrame.sum()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.sum.html#pandas.DataFrame.sum) also show “unused” categories when `observed=False`.

```
In [138]: columns = pd.Categorical(
   .....:     ["One", "One", "Two"], categories=["One", "Two", "Three"], ordered=True
   .....: )
   .....: 
In [139]: df = pd.DataFrame(
   .....:     data=[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]],
   .....:     columns=pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([["A", "B", "B"], columns]),
   .....: ).T
   .....: 
In [140]: df.groupby(level=1, observed=False).sum()
Out[140]: 
       0  1
One    3  9
Two    3  6
Three  0  0
```
Groupby will also show “unused” categories when `observed=False`:

```
In [141]: cats = pd.Categorical(
   .....:     ["a", "b", "b", "b", "c", "c", "c"], categories=["a", "b", "c", "d"]
   .....: )
   .....: 
In [142]: df = pd.DataFrame({"cats": cats, "values": [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5]})

In [142]: df = pd.DataFrame({"cats": cats, "values": [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5]})

cats

cats B        
a    c     1.0

Pivot tables:

```
In [147]: raw_cat = pd.Categorical(["a", "a", "b", "b"], categories=["a", "b", "c"])
In [148]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": raw_cat, "B": ["c", "d", "c", "d"], "values": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
In [149]: pd.pivot_table(df, values="values", index=["A", "B"], observed=False)
Out[149]:

A B        
a c     1.0
  d     2.0
b c     3.0
  d     4.0
```

payload.content:
## Data munging[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#data-munging)

The optimized pandas data access methods  `.loc`, `.iloc`, `.at`, and `.iat`,
work as normal. The only difference is the return type (for getting) and
that only values already in `categories` can be assigned.

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming > Getting[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#getting)
payload.content:
## Getting[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#getting)

If the slicing operation returns either a `DataFrame` or a column of type
`Series`, the `category` dtype is preserved.

```
In [150]: idx = pd.Index(["h", "i", "j", "k", "l", "m", "n"])
In [151]: cats = pd.Series(["a", "b", "b", "b", "c", "c", "c"], dtype="category", index=idx)
In [152]: values = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5]
In [153]: df = pd.DataFrame({"cats": cats, "values": values}, index=idx)
In [154]: df.iloc[2:4, :]
Out[154]: 
  cats  values
j    b       2
k    b       2
In [155]: df.iloc[2:4, :].dtypes
Out[155]: 
cats      category
values       int64
dtype: object
In [156]: df.loc["h":"j", "cats"]
Out[156]: 
h    a
i    b
j    b
Name: cats, dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
In [157]: df[df["cats"] == "b"]
Out[157]: 
  cats  values
i    b       2
j    b       2
k    b       2
```
An example where the category type is not preserved is if you take one single
row: the resulting `Series` is of dtype `object`:

```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.section: get the complete "h" row as a Series
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > get the complete "h" row as a Series
payload.content:
## get the complete "h" row as a Series

In [158]: df.loc["h", :]
Out[158]: 
cats      a
values    1
Name: h, dtype: object
```
Returning a single item from categorical data will also return the value, not a categorical of length “1”.

```
In [159]: df.iat[0, 0]
Out[159]: 'a'
In [160]: df["cats"] = df["cats"].cat.rename_categories(["x", "y", "z"])
In [161]: df.at["h", "cats"]  # returns a string
Out[161]: 'x'
```
Note

This is in contrast to R’s `factor` function, where `factor(c(1,2,3))[1]`
returns a single value `factor`.

To get a single value `Series` of type `category`, you pass in a list with
a single value:

```
In [162]: df.loc[["h"], "cats"]
Out[162]: 
h    x
Name: cats, dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['x', 'y', 'z']
```

payload.content:
## String and datetime accessors[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#string-and-datetime-accessors)

The accessors  `.dt` and `.str` will work if the `s.cat.categories` are of
an appropriate type:

```
In [163]: str_s = pd.Series(list("aabb"))
In [164]: str_cat = str_s.astype("category")
In [165]: str_cat
Out[165]: 
0    a
1    a
2    b
3    b
dtype: category
Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']
In [166]: str_cat.str.contains("a")
Out[166]: 
0     True
1     True
2    False
3    False
dtype: bool
In [167]: date_s = pd.Series(pd.date_range("1/1/2015", periods=5))
In [168]: date_cat = date_s.astype("category")
In [169]: date_cat
Out[169]: 
0   2015-01-01
1   2015-01-02
2   2015-01-03
3   2015-01-04
4   2015-01-05
dtype: category
Categories (5, datetime64[us]): [2015-01-01, 2015-01-02, 2015-01-03, 2015-01-04,
                                 2015-01-05]
In [170]: date_cat.dt.day
Out[170]: 
0    1
1    2
2    3
3    4
4    5
dtype: int32
```
Note

The returned `Series` (or `DataFrame`) is of the same type as if you used the
`.str.<method>` / `.dt.<method>` on a `Series` of that type (and not of
type `category`!).

That means, that the returned values from methods and properties on the accessors of a
`Series` and the returned values from methods and properties on the accessors of this
`Series` transformed to one of type `category` will be equal:

```
In [171]: ret_s = str_s.str.contains("a")
In [172]: ret_cat = str_cat.str.contains("a")
In [173]: ret_s.dtype == ret_cat.dtype
Out[173]: True
In [174]: ret_s == ret_cat
Out[174]: 
0    True
1    True
2    True
3    True
dtype: bool
```
Note

The work is done on the `categories` and then a new `Series` is constructed. This has
some performance implication if you have a `Series` of type string, where lots of elements

payload.content:
Out[174]: 
0    True
1    True
2    True
3    True
dtype: bool
```
Note

The work is done on the `categories` and then a new `Series` is constructed. This has
some performance implication if you have a `Series` of type string, where lots of elements
are repeated (i.e. the number of unique elements in the `Series` is a lot smaller than the
length of the `Series`). In this case it can be faster to convert the original `Series`
to one of type `category` and use `.str.<method>` or `.dt.<property>` on that.

payload.content:
## Setting[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#setting)

Setting values in a categorical column (or `Series`) works as long as the
value is included in the `categories`:

```
In [175]: idx = pd.Index(["h", "i", "j", "k", "l", "m", "n"])
In [176]: cats = pd.Categorical(["a", "a", "a", "a", "a", "a", "a"], categories=["a", "b"])
In [177]: values = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
In [178]: df = pd.DataFrame({"cats": cats, "values": values}, index=idx)
In [179]: df.iloc[2:4, :] = [["b", 2], ["b", 2]]
In [180]: df
Out[180]: 
  cats  values
h    a       1
i    a       1
j    b       2
k    b       2
l    a       1
m    a       1
n    a       1
In [181]: try:
   .....:     df.iloc[2:4, :] = [["c", 3], ["c", 3]]
   .....: except TypeError as e:
   .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
   .....: 
TypeError: Cannot setitem on a Categorical with a new category, set the categories first
```
Setting values by assigning categorical data will also check that the `categories` match:

```
In [182]: df.loc["j":"k", "cats"] = pd.Categorical(["a", "a"], categories=["a", "b"])
In [183]: df
Out[183]: 
  cats  values
h    a       1
i    a       1
j    a       2
k    a       2
l    a       1
m    a       1
n    a       1
In [184]: try:
   .....:     df.loc["j":"k", "cats"] = pd.Categorical(["b", "b"], categories=["a", "b", "c"])
   .....: except TypeError as e:
   .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
   .....: 
TypeError: Cannot set a Categorical with another, without identical categories
```
Assigning a `Categorical` to parts of a column of other types will use the values:

```
In [185]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 1, 1, 1, 1], "b": ["a", "a", "a", "a", "a"]})
In [186]: df.loc[1:2, "a"] = pd.Categorical([2, 2], categories=[2, 3])

payload.content:
```
Assigning a `Categorical` to parts of a column of other types will use the values:

```
In [185]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 1, 1, 1, 1], "b": ["a", "a", "a", "a", "a"]})
In [186]: df.loc[1:2, "a"] = pd.Categorical([2, 2], categories=[2, 3])
In [187]: df.loc[2:3, "b"] = pd.Categorical(["b", "b"], categories=["a", "b"])
In [188]: df
Out[188]: 
   a  b
0  1  a
1  2  a
2  2  b
3  1  b
4  1  a
In [189]: df.dtypes
Out[189]: 
a    int64
b      str
dtype: object
```
Note

The examples above use `.loc` / `.iloc` to set values *within* an
existing categorical column, which preserves the `category` dtype.
Assigning to a full column with `df["cats"] = value` instead **replaces**
the column, so the dtype is inferred from `value` rather than kept. See
[Column assignment vs. in-place setting](https://pandas.pydata.org/indexing.html#indexing-column-assignment-vs-in-place) for details.

payload.content:
## Merging / concatenation[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#merging-concatenation)

By default, combining `Series` or `DataFrames` which contain the same
categories results in `category` dtype, otherwise results will depend on the
dtype of the underlying categories. Merges that result in non-categorical
dtypes will likely have higher memory usage. Use `union_categories=True`,
`.astype` or `union_categoricals` to ensure `category` results.

```
In [190]: from pandas.api.types import union_categoricals

payload.content:
## same categories

In [191]: s1 = pd.Series(["a", "b"], dtype="category")
In [192]: s2 = pd.Series(["a", "b", "a"], dtype="category")
In [193]: pd.concat([s1, s2])
Out[193]: 
0    a
1    b
0    a
1    b
2    a
dtype: category
Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > different categories
payload.content:
## different categories

In [194]: s3 = pd.Series(["b", "c"], dtype="category")
In [195]: pd.concat([s1, s3])
Out[195]: 
0    a
1    b
0    b
1    c
dtype: str

payload.section: Output dtype is inferred based on categories values
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Output dtype is inferred based on categories values
payload.content:
## Output dtype is inferred based on categories values

In [196]: int_cats = pd.Series([1, 2], dtype="category")
In [197]: float_cats = pd.Series([3.0, 4.0], dtype="category")
In [198]: pd.concat([int_cats, float_cats])
Out[198]: 
0    1.0
1    2.0
0    3.0
1    4.0
dtype: float64
In [199]: pd.concat([s1, s3], union_categories=True)
Out[199]: 
0    a
1    b
0    b
1    c
dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
In [200]: pd.concat([int_cats, float_cats], union_categories=True)
Out[200]: 
0    1.0
1    2.0
0    3.0
1    4.0
dtype: category
Categories (4, float64): [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
In [201]: pd.concat([s1, s3]).astype("category")
Out[201]: 
0    a
1    b
0    b
1    c
dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
In [202]: union_categoricals([s1.array, s3.array])
Out[202]: 
['a', 'b', 'b', 'c']
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
```
The following table summarizes the results of merging `Categoricals`:

| arg1 | arg2 | identical | result | 
|---|---|---|---|
| category | category | True | category | 
| category (object) | category (object) | False | object (dtype is inferred) | 
| category (int) | category (float) | False | float (dtype is inferred) |

payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Output dtype is inferred based on categories values > Unioning[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#unioning)
payload.content:
## Unioning[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#unioning)

If you want to combine categoricals that do not necessarily have the same
categories, the [`union_categoricals()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.api.types.union_categoricals.html#pandas.api.types.union_categoricals) function will
combine a list-like of categoricals. The new categories will be the union of
the categories being combined.

```
In [203]: from pandas.api.types import union_categoricals
In [204]: a = pd.Categorical(["b", "c"])
In [205]: b = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"])
In [206]: union_categoricals([a, b])
Out[206]: 
['b', 'c', 'a', 'b']
Categories (3, str): ['b', 'c', 'a']
```
By default, the resulting categories will be ordered as
they appear in the data. If you want the categories to
be lexsorted, use `sort_categories=True` argument.

```
In [207]: union_categoricals([a, b], sort_categories=True)
Out[207]: 
['b', 'c', 'a', 'b']
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'c']
```
`union_categoricals` also works with the “easy” case of combining two
categoricals of the same categories and order information
(e.g. what you could also `append` for).

```
In [208]: a = pd.Categorical(["a", "b"], ordered=True)
In [209]: b = pd.Categorical(["a", "b", "a"], ordered=True)
In [210]: union_categoricals([a, b])

## Getting data in/out[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#getting-data-in-out)

You can write data that contains `category` dtypes to a `HDFStore`.
See [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/io.html#io-hdf5-categorical) for an example and caveats.

categorical (categories and ordering). So if you read back the CSV file you have to convert the
relevant columns back to `category` and assign the right categories and categories ordering.

```

payload.content:
## Missing data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#missing-data)

pandas primarily uses the value `np.nan` to represent missing data. It is by
default not included in computations. See [Working with missing data](https://pandas.pydata.org/missing_data.html#missing-data).

Missing values should **not** be included in the Categorical’s `categories`,
only in the `values`.
Instead, it is understood that NaN is different, and is always a possibility.
When working with the Categorical’s `codes`, missing values will always have
a code of `-1`.

```
In [243]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", np.nan, "a"], dtype="category")

1      b
2    NaN
3      a
dtype: category
Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']
In [245]: s.cat.codes
Out[245]: 
0    0
1    1
2   -1
3    0
dtype: int8
```
Methods for working with missing data, e.g. [`isna()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.isna.html#pandas.Series.isna), [`fillna()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.fillna.html#pandas.Series.fillna),
[`dropna()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.dropna.html#pandas.Series.dropna), all work normally:

```
In [246]: s = pd.Series(["a", "b", np.nan], dtype="category")
In [247]: s
Out[247]: 
0      a
1      b
2    NaN
dtype: category
Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']
In [248]: pd.isna(s)
Out[248]: 
0    False
1    False
2     True
dtype: bool
In [249]: s.fillna("a")
Out[249]: 
0    a
1    b
2    a
dtype: category
Categories (2, str): ['a', 'b']
```

payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > only two categories > Differences to R’s `factor`[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#differences-to-r-s-factor)
payload.content:
## Differences to R’s `factor`[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#differences-to-r-s-factor)

The following differences to R’s factor functions can be observed:

- R’s `levels` are named `categories`.
- R’s `levels` are always of type string, while `categories` in pandas can be of any dtype.
- It’s not possible to specify labels at creation time. Use `s.cat.rename_categories(new_labels)` afterwards.
- In contrast to R’s `factor` function, using categorical data as the sole input to create a
new categorical series will *not* remove unused categories but create a new categorical series
which is equal to the passed in one!
- R allows for missing values to be included in its `levels` (pandas’ `categories`). pandas
does not allow `NaN` categories, but missing values can still be in the `values`.

## Memory usage[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#memory-usage)

The memory usage of a `Categorical` is proportional to the number *and size* of categories plus the length of the data. In contrast,
an `object` dtype is proportional to the size of the objects times the length of the data.

```
In [250]: s = pd.Series(["foo", "bar"] * 1000, dtype="object")

payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > category dtype > `Categorical` is not a `numpy` array[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categorical-is-not-a-numpy-array)
payload.content:
## `Categorical` is not a `numpy` array[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categorical-is-not-a-numpy-array)

Currently, categorical data and the underlying `Categorical` is implemented as a Python
object and not as a low-level NumPy array dtype. This leads to some problems.

NumPy itself doesn’t know about the new `dtype`:

```
In [256]: try:
   .....:     np.dtype("category")
   .....: except TypeError as e:
   .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
   .....: 
TypeError: data type 'category' not understood
In [257]: dtype = pd.Categorical(["a"]).dtype
In [258]: try:
   .....:     np.dtype(dtype)
   .....: except TypeError as e:
   .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
   .....: 
TypeError: Cannot interpret 'CategoricalDtype(categories=['a'], ordered=False, categories_dtype=str)' as a data type
```
Dtype comparisons work:

```
In [259]: dtype == np.str_
Out[259]: False
In [260]: np.str_ == dtype
Out[260]: False
```
To check if a Series contains Categorical data, use `hasattr(s, 'cat')`:

```
In [261]: hasattr(pd.Series(["a"], dtype="category"), "cat")
Out[261]: True
In [262]: hasattr(pd.Series(["a"]), "cat")
Out[262]: False
```
Using NumPy functions on a `Series` of type `category` should not work as `Categoricals`
are not numeric data (even in the case that `.categories` is numeric).

```
In [263]: s = pd.Series(pd.Categorical([1, 2, 3, 4]))
In [264]: try:
   .....:     np.sum(s)
   .....: except TypeError as e:
   .....:     print("TypeError:", str(e))
   .....: 
TypeError: 'Categorical' with dtype category does not support operation 'sum'
```

payload.title: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Categorical data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > category dtype > dtype in apply[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#dtype-in-apply)
payload.content:
## dtype in apply[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#dtype-in-apply)

pandas currently does not preserve the dtype in apply functions: If you apply along rows you get
a `Series` of `object` `dtype` (same as getting a row -> getting one element will return a
basic type) and applying along columns will also convert to object. `NaN` values are unaffected.
You can use `fillna` to handle missing values before applying a function.

```
In [265]: df = pd.DataFrame(
   .....:     {
   .....:         "a": [1, 2, 3, 4],
   .....:         "b": ["a", "b", "c", "d"],
   .....:         "cats": pd.Categorical([1, 2, 3, 2]),
   .....:     }
   .....: )
   .....: 
In [266]: df.apply(lambda row: type(row["cats"]), axis=1)
Out[266]: 
0    <class 'int'>
1    <class 'int'>
2    <class 'int'>
3    <class 'int'>
dtype: object
In [267]: df.apply(lambda col: col.dtype, axis=0)
Out[267]: 
a          int64
b            str
cats    category
dtype: object
```

payload.content:
## Categorical index[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categorical-index)

`CategoricalIndex` is a type of index that is useful for supporting
indexing with duplicates. This is a container around a `Categorical`
and allows efficient indexing and storage of an index with a large number of duplicated elements.
See the [advanced indexing docs](https://pandas.pydata.org/advanced.html#advanced-categoricalindex) for a more detailed
explanation.

Setting the index will create a `CategoricalIndex`:

```
In [268]: cats = pd.Categorical([1, 2, 3, 4], categories=[4, 2, 3, 1])
In [269]: strings = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
In [270]: values = [4, 2, 3, 1]
In [271]: df = pd.DataFrame({"strings": strings, "values": values}, index=cats)
In [272]: df.index
Out[272]: 
CategoricalIndex([1, 2, 3, 4], categories=[4, 2, 3, 1], ordered=False,
                 dtype='category')

payload.title: Nullable integer data type — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Nullable integer data type — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Nullable integer data type[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#nullable-integer-data-type)
payload.content:
## Nullable integer data type[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#nullable-integer-data-type)

[`arrays.IntegerArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.arrays.IntegerArray.html#pandas.arrays.IntegerArray) uses [`pandas.NA`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.NA.html#pandas.NA) as its missing value.

In [Working with missing data](https://pandas.pydata.org/missing_data.html#missing-data), we saw that pandas primarily uses `NaN` to represent
missing data. Because `NaN` is a float, this forces an array of integers with
any missing values to become floating point. In some cases, this may not matter
much. But if your integer column is, say, an identifier, casting to float can
be problematic. Some integers cannot even be represented as floating point
numbers.

payload.title: Nullable integer data type — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Nullable integer data type — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Nullable integer data type[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#nullable-integer-data-type) > Construction[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#construction)
payload.content:
## Construction[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#construction)

pandas can represent integer data with possibly missing values using
[`arrays.IntegerArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.arrays.IntegerArray.html#pandas.arrays.IntegerArray). This is an [extension type](https://pandas.pydata.org/development/extending.html#extending-extension-types)
implemented within pandas.

```
In [1]: arr = pd.array([1, 2, None], dtype=pd.Int64Dtype())
In [2]: arr
Out[2]: 
<IntegerArray>
[1, 2, <NA>]
Length: 3, dtype: Int64
```
Or the string alias `"Int64"` (note the capital `"I"`) to differentiate from
NumPy’s `'int64'` dtype:

```
In [3]: pd.array([1, 2, np.nan], dtype="Int64")
Out[3]: 
<IntegerArray>
[1, 2, <NA>]
Length: 3, dtype: Int64
```
All NA-like values are replaced with [`pandas.NA`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.NA.html#pandas.NA).

```
In [4]: pd.array([1, 2, np.nan, None, pd.NA], dtype="Int64")
Out[4]: 
<IntegerArray>
[1, 2, <NA>, <NA>, <NA>]
Length: 5, dtype: Int64
```
This array can be stored in a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) or [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) like any
NumPy array.

```
In [5]: pd.Series(arr)
Out[5]: 
0       1
1       2
2    <NA>
dtype: Int64
```
You can also pass the list-like object to the [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) constructor
with the dtype.

Warning

Currently [`pandas.array()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.array.html#pandas.array) and [`pandas.Series()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) use different

payload.title: Nullable integer data type — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Nullable integer data type — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Nullable integer data type[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#nullable-integer-data-type) > Construction[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#construction)
payload.content:
with the dtype.

Warning

Currently [`pandas.array()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.array.html#pandas.array) and [`pandas.Series()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) use different
rules for dtype inference. [`pandas.array()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.array.html#pandas.array) will infer a
nullable-integer dtype

```
In [6]: pd.array([1, None])
Out[6]: 
<IntegerArray>
[1, <NA>]
Length: 2, dtype: Int64
In [7]: pd.array([1, 2])
Out[7]: 
<IntegerArray>
[1, 2]
Length: 2, dtype: Int64
```
For backwards-compatibility, [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) infers these as either
integer or float dtype.

```
In [8]: pd.Series([1, None])
Out[8]: 
0    1.0
1    NaN
dtype: float64
In [9]: pd.Series([1, 2])
Out[9]: 
0    1
1    2
dtype: int64
```
We recommend explicitly providing the dtype to avoid confusion.

```
In [10]: pd.array([1, None], dtype="Int64")
Out[10]: 
<IntegerArray>
[1, <NA>]
Length: 2, dtype: Int64
In [11]: pd.Series([1, None], dtype="Int64")
Out[11]: 
0       1
1    <NA>
dtype: Int64
```
In the future, we may provide an option for [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) to infer a
nullable-integer dtype.

If you create a column of `NA` values (for example to fill them later)
with `df['new_col'] = pd.NA`, the `dtype` would be set to `object` in the
new column. The performance on this column will be worse than with
the appropriate type. It’s better to use
`df['new_col'] = pd.Series(pd.NA, dtype="Int64")`
(or another `dtype` that supports `NA`).

```
In [12]: df = pd.DataFrame()
In [13]: df['objects'] = pd.NA
In [14]: df.dtypes
Out[14]: 
objects    object
dtype: object
```

payload.content:
## Indexing with NA values[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-with-na-values)

pandas allows indexing with `NA` values in a boolean array, which are treated as `False`.

```
In [1]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
In [2]: mask = pd.array([True, False, pd.NA], dtype="boolean")
In [3]: s[mask]
Out[3]: 
0    1
dtype: int64
```
If you would prefer to keep the `NA` values you can manually fill them with `fillna(True)`.

```
In [4]: s[mask.fillna(True)]
Out[4]: 
0    1
2    3
dtype: int64
```
If you create a column of `NA` values (for example to fill them later)
with `df['new_col'] = pd.NA`, the `dtype` would be set to `object` in the
new column. The performance on this column will be worse than with
the appropriate type. It’s better to use
`df['new_col'] = pd.Series(pd.NA, dtype="boolean")`
(or another `dtype` that supports `NA`).

```
In [5]: df = pd.DataFrame()
In [6]: df['objects'] = pd.NA
In [7]: df.dtypes
Out[7]: 
objects    object
dtype: object
```

payload.content:
## Kleene logical operations[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#kleene-logical-operations)

[`arrays.BooleanArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.arrays.BooleanArray.html#pandas.arrays.BooleanArray) implements [Kleene Logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-valued_logic#Kleene_and_Priest_logics) (sometimes called three-value logic) for
logical operations like `&` (and), `|` (or) and `^` (exclusive-or).

This table demonstrates the results for every combination. These operations are symmetrical, so flipping the left- and right-hand side makes no difference in the result.

| Expression | Result | 
|---|---|
| `True & True` | `True` | 
| `True & False` | `False` | 
| `True & NA` | `NA` | 
| `False & False` | `False` | 
| `False & NA` | `False` | 
| `NA & NA` | `NA` | 
| `True \| True` | `True` | 
| `True \| False` | `True` | 
| `True \| NA` | `True` | 
| `False \| False` | `False` | 
| `False \| NA` | `NA` | 
| `NA \| NA` | `NA` | 
| `True ^ True` | `False` | 
| `True ^ False` | `True` | 
| `True ^ NA` | `NA` | 
| `False ^ False` | `False` | 
| `False ^ NA` | `NA` | 
| `NA ^ NA` | `NA` | 

When an `NA` is present in an operation, the output value is `NA` only if
the result cannot be determined solely based on the other input. For example,
`True | NA` is `True`, because both `True | True` and `True | False`
are `True`. In that case, we don’t actually need to consider the value
of the `NA`.

On the other hand, `True & NA` is `NA`. The result depends on whether
the `NA` really is `True` or `False`, since `True & True` is `True`,
but `True & False` is `False`, so we can’t determine the output.

This differs from how `np.nan` behaves in logical operations. pandas treated
`np.nan` is *always false in the output*.

In `or`

```

payload.content:
## Chart visualization[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#chart-visualization)

This section demonstrates visualization through charting. For information on
visualization of tabular data please see the section on [Table Visualization](https://pandas.pydata.org/style.html).

We use the standard convention for referencing the matplotlib API:

```
In [1]: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
In [2]: plt.close("all")
```
We provide the basics in pandas to easily create decent looking plots.
See [the ecosystem page](https://pandas.pydata.org/community/ecosystem.html) for visualization
libraries that go beyond the basics documented here.

Note

All calls to `np.random` are seeded with 123456.

payload.title: Chart visualization — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Chart visualization — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Chart visualization[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#chart-visualization) > Basic plotting: `plot`[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#basic-plotting-plot)
payload.content:
## Basic plotting: `plot`[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#basic-plotting-plot)

We will demonstrate the basics, see the [cookbook](https://pandas.pydata.org/cookbook.html#cookbook-plotting) for
some advanced strategies.

The `plot` method on Series and DataFrame is just a simple wrapper around
[`plt.plot()`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.axes.Axes.plot.html#matplotlib.axes.Axes.plot):

```
In [3]: np.random.seed(123456)
In [4]: ts = pd.Series(np.random.randn(1000), index=pd.date_range("1/1/2000", periods=1000))
In [5]: ts = ts.cumsum()
In [6]: ts.plot();
```
If the index consists of dates, it calls [`gcf().autofmt_xdate()`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.figure.Figure.autofmt_xdate.html#matplotlib.figure.Figure.autofmt_xdate)
to try to format the x-axis nicely as per above.

On DataFrame, [`plot()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot) is a convenience to plot all of the columns with labels:

```
In [7]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(1000, 4), index=ts.index, columns=list("ABCD"))
In [8]: df = df.cumsum()
In [9]: plt.figure();
In [10]: df.plot();
```
You can plot one column versus another using the `x` and `y` keywords in
[`plot()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot):

```
In [11]: df3 = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(1000, 2), columns=["B", "C"]).cumsum()
In [12]: df3["A"] = pd.Series(list(range(len(df))))
In [13]: df3.plot(x="A", y="B");
```

payload.content:
## Other plots[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#other-plots)

Plotting methods allow for a handful of plot styles other than the
default line plot. These methods can be provided as the `kind`
keyword argument to [`plot()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot), and include:

- [‘bar’](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-barplot) or [‘barh’](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-barplot) for bar plots
- [‘hist’](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-hist) for histogram
- [‘box’](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-box) for boxplot
- [‘kde’](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-kde) or [‘density’](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-kde) for density plots
- [‘area’](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-area-plot) for area plots
- [‘scatter’](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-scatter) for scatter plots
- [‘hexbin’](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-hexbin) for hexagonal bin plots
- [‘pie’](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-pie) for pie plots

For example, a bar plot can be created the following way:

```
In [14]: plt.figure();
In [15]: df.iloc[5].plot(kind="bar");
```
You can also create these other plots using the methods `DataFrame.plot.<kind>` instead of providing the `kind` keyword argument. This makes it easier to discover plot methods and the specific arguments they use:

```
In [16]: df = pd.DataFrame()
In [17]: df.plot.<TAB>  # noqa: E225, E999
df.plot.area     df.plot.barh     df.plot.density  df.plot.hist     df.plot.line     df.plot.scatter
df.plot.bar      df.plot.box      df.plot.hexbin   df.plot.kde      df.plot.pie
```
In addition to these `kind` s, there are the [DataFrame.hist()](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-hist),

payload.content:
df.plot.bar      df.plot.box      df.plot.hexbin   df.plot.kde      df.plot.pie
```
In addition to these `kind` s, there are the [DataFrame.hist()](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-hist),
and [DataFrame.boxplot()](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-box) methods, which use a separate interface.

Finally, there are several [plotting functions](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-tools) in `pandas.plotting`
that take a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) or [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) as an argument. These
include:

- [Scatter Matrix](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-scatter-matrix)
- [Andrews Curves](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-andrews-curves)
- [Parallel Coordinates](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-parallel-coordinates)
- [Lag Plot](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-lag)
- [Autocorrelation Plot](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-autocorrelation)
- [Bootstrap Plot](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-bootstrap)
- [RadViz](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-radviz)

Plots may also be adorned with [errorbars](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-errorbars)
or [tables](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-table).

payload.content:
## Bar plots[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#bar-plots)

For labeled, non-time series data, you may wish to produce a bar plot:

```
In [18]: plt.figure();
In [19]: df.iloc[5].plot.bar();
In [20]: plt.axhline(0, color="k");
```
Calling a DataFrame’s [`plot.bar()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.bar.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot.bar) method produces a multiple
bar plot:

```
In [21]: df2 = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(10, 4), columns=["a", "b", "c", "d"])
In [22]: df2.plot.bar();
```
To produce a stacked bar plot, pass `stacked=True`:

```
In [23]: df2.plot.bar(stacked=True);
```
To get horizontal bar plots, use the `barh` method:

```
In [24]: df2.plot.barh(stacked=True);
```

payload.content:
## Histograms[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#histograms)

Histograms can be drawn by using the [`DataFrame.plot.hist()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.hist.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot.hist) and [`Series.plot.hist()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.plot.hist.html#pandas.Series.plot.hist) methods.

```
In [25]: df4 = pd.DataFrame(
   ....:     {
   ....:         "a": np.random.randn(1000) + 1,
   ....:         "b": np.random.randn(1000),
   ....:         "c": np.random.randn(1000) - 1,
   ....:     },
   ....:     columns=["a", "b", "c"],
   ....: )
   ....: 
In [26]: plt.figure();
In [27]: df4.plot.hist(alpha=0.5);
```
A histogram can be stacked using `stacked=True`. Bin size can be changed
using the `bins` keyword.

```
In [28]: plt.figure();
In [29]: df4.plot.hist(stacked=True, bins=20);
```
You can pass other keywords supported by matplotlib `hist`. For example,
horizontal and cumulative histograms can be drawn by
`orientation='horizontal'` and `cumulative=True`.

```
In [30]: plt.figure();
In [31]: df4["a"].plot.hist(orientation="horizontal", cumulative=True);
```
See the [`hist`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.axes.Axes.hist.html#matplotlib.axes.Axes.hist) method and the
[matplotlib hist documentation](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.hist.html) for more.

The existing interface `DataFrame.hist` to plot histogram still can be used.

```
In [32]: plt.figure();
In [33]: df["A"].diff().hist();
```
[`DataFrame.hist()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.hist.html#pandas.DataFrame.hist) plots the histograms of the columns on multiple
subplots:

```
In [34]: plt.figure();
In [35]: df.diff().hist(color="k", alpha=0.5, bins=50);
```

## Box plots[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#box-plots)

Boxplot can be drawn calling [`Series.plot.box()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.plot.box.html#pandas.Series.plot.box) and [`DataFrame.plot.box()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.box.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot.box),
or [`DataFrame.boxplot()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.boxplot.html#pandas.DataFrame.boxplot) to visualize the distribution of values within each column.

For instance, here is a boxplot representing five trials of 10 observations of a uniform random variable on \[0,1).

```
In [40]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(10, 5), columns=["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"])
In [41]: df.plot.box();
```
Boxplot can be colorized by passing `color` keyword. You can pass a `dict`
whose keys are `boxes`, `whiskers`, `medians` and `caps`.
If some keys are missing in the `dict`, default colors are used
for the corresponding artists. Also, boxplot has `sym` keyword to specify fliers style.

When you pass other type of arguments via `color` keyword, it will be directly
passed to matplotlib for all the `boxes`, `whiskers`, `medians` and `caps`
colorization.

The colors are applied to every boxes to be drawn. If you want
more complicated colorization, you can get each drawn artists by passing
[return\_type](https://pandas.pydata.org#visualization-box-return).

```
In [42]: color = {
   ....:     "boxes": "DarkGreen",
   ....:     "whiskers": "DarkOrange",
   ....:     "medians": "DarkBlue",
   ....:     "caps": "Gray",
   ....: }
   ....: 
In [43]: df.plot.box(color=color, sym="r+");
```
Also, you can pass other keywords supported by matplotlib `boxplot`.
For example, horizontal and custom-positioned boxplot can be drawn by

....:     "caps": "Gray",
   ....: }
   ....: 
In [43]: df.plot.box(color=color, sym="r+");
```
Also, you can pass other keywords supported by matplotlib `boxplot`.
For example, horizontal and custom-positioned boxplot can be drawn by
`vert=False` and `positions` keywords.

```
In [44]: df.plot.box(vert=False, positions=[1, 4, 5, 6, 8]);
```
See the [`boxplot`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.axes.Axes.boxplot.html#matplotlib.axes.Axes.boxplot) method and the
[matplotlib boxplot documentation](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.boxplot.html) for more.

You can create a stratified boxplot using the `by` keyword argument to create
groupings.  For instance,

```
In [48]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(10, 2), columns=["Col1", "Col2"])

```
In [52]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(10, 3), columns=["Col1", "Col2", "Col3"])

payload.content:
In [56]: bp = df.boxplot(column=["Col1", "Col2"], by=["X", "Y"])
```
You could also create groupings with [`DataFrame.plot.box()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.box.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot.box), for instance:

```
In [57]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(10, 3), columns=["Col1", "Col2", "Col3"])
In [58]: df["X"] = pd.Series(["A", "A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B"])
In [59]: plt.figure();
In [60]: bp = df.plot.box(column=["Col1", "Col2"], by="X")
```
In `boxplot`, the return type can be controlled by the `return_type`, keyword. The valid choices are `{"axes", "dict", "both", None}`.
Faceting, created by `DataFrame.boxplot` with the `by`
keyword, will affect the output type as well:

| `return_type` | Faceted | Output type | 
|---|---|---|
| `None` | No | axes | 
| `None` | Yes | 2-D ndarray of axes | 
| `'axes'` | No | axes | 
| `'axes'` | Yes | Series of axes | 
| `'dict'` | No | dict of artists | 
| `'dict'` | Yes | Series of dicts of artists | 
| `'both'` | No | namedtuple | 
| `'both'` | Yes | Series of namedtuples | 

`Groupby.boxplot` always returns a `Series` of `return_type`.

```
In [61]: np.random.seed(1234)
In [62]: df_box = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(50, 2))
In [63]: df_box["g"] = np.random.choice(["A", "B"], size=50)
In [64]: df_box.loc[df_box["g"] == "B", 1] += 3
In [65]: bp = df_box.boxplot(by="g")
```
The subplots above are split by the numeric columns first, then the value of
the `g` column. Below the subplots are first split by the value of `g`,
then by the numeric columns.

```
In [66]: bp = df_box.groupby("g").boxplot()
```

payload.content:
## Area plot[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#area-plot)

You can create area plots with [`Series.plot.area()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.plot.area.html#pandas.Series.plot.area) and [`DataFrame.plot.area()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.area.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot.area).
Area plots are stacked by default. To produce stacked area plot, each column must be either all positive or all negative values.

When input data contains `NaN`, it will be automatically filled by 0. If you want to drop or fill by different values, use `dataframe.dropna()` or `dataframe.fillna()` before calling `plot`.

```
In [67]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(10, 4), columns=["a", "b", "c", "d"])
In [68]: df.plot.area();
```
To produce an unstacked plot, pass `stacked=False`. Alpha value is set to 0.5 unless otherwise specified:

```
In [69]: df.plot.area(stacked=False);
```

payload.content:
## Scatter plot[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#scatter-plot)

Scatter plot can be drawn by using the [`DataFrame.plot.scatter()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.scatter.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot.scatter) method.
Scatter plot requires numeric columns for the x and y axes.
These can be specified by the `x` and `y` keywords.

```
In [70]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(50, 4), columns=["a", "b", "c", "d"])
In [71]: df["species"] = pd.Categorical(
   ....:     ["setosa"] * 20 + ["versicolor"] * 20 + ["virginica"] * 10
   ....: )
   ....: 
In [72]: df.plot.scatter(x="a", y="b");
```
To plot multiple column groups in a single axes, repeat `plot` method specifying target `ax`.
It is recommended to specify `color` and `label` keywords to distinguish each groups.

```
In [73]: ax = df.plot.scatter(x="a", y="b", color="DarkBlue", label="Group 1")
In [74]: df.plot.scatter(x="c", y="d", color="DarkGreen", label="Group 2", ax=ax);
```
The keyword `c` may be given as the name of a column to provide colors for
each point:

```
In [75]: df.plot.scatter(x="a", y="b", c="c", s=50);
```
If a categorical column is passed to `c`, then a discrete colorbar will be produced:

```
In [76]: df.plot.scatter(x="a", y="b", c="species", cmap="viridis", s=50);
```
You can pass other keywords supported by matplotlib
[`scatter`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.axes.Axes.scatter.html#matplotlib.axes.Axes.scatter). The example  below shows a
bubble chart using a column of the `DataFrame` as the bubble size.

```
In [77]: df.plot.scatter(x="a", y="b", s=df["c"] * 200);
```
See the [`scatter`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.axes.Axes.scatter.html#matplotlib.axes.Axes.scatter) method and the

payload.breadcrumb: Chart visualization — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Chart visualization[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#chart-visualization) > Hexagonal bin plot[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#hexagonal-bin-plot)
payload.content:
## Hexagonal bin plot[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#hexagonal-bin-plot)

You can create hexagonal bin plots with [`DataFrame.plot.hexbin()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.hexbin.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot.hexbin).
Hexbin plots can be a useful alternative to scatter plots if your data are
too dense to plot each point individually.

```
In [78]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(1000, 2), columns=["a", "b"])
In [79]: df["b"] = df["b"] + np.arange(1000)
In [80]: df.plot.hexbin(x="a", y="b", gridsize=25);
```
A useful keyword argument is `gridsize`; it controls the number of hexagons
in the x-direction, and defaults to 100. A larger `gridsize` means more, smaller
bins.

By default, a histogram of the counts around each `(x, y)` point is computed.
You can specify alternative aggregations by passing values to the `C` and
`reduce_C_function` arguments. `C` specifies the value at each `(x, y)` point
and `reduce_C_function` is a function of one argument that reduces all the
values in a bin to a single number (e.g. `mean`, `max`, `sum`, `std`).  In this
example the positions are given by columns `a` and `b`, while the value is
given by column `z`. The bins are aggregated with NumPy’s `max` function.

```
In [81]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(1000, 2), columns=["a", "b"])
In [82]: df["b"] = df["b"] + np.arange(1000)
In [83]: df["z"] = np.random.uniform(0, 3, 1000)
In [84]: df.plot.hexbin(x="a", y="b", C="z", reduce_C_function=np.max, gridsize=25);
```
See the [`hexbin`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.axes.Axes.hexbin.html#matplotlib.axes.Axes.hexbin) method and the
[matplotlib hexbin documentation](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.hexbin.html) for more.

payload.content:
## Pie plot[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#pie-plot)

You can create a pie plot with [`DataFrame.plot.pie()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.pie.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot.pie) or [`Series.plot.pie()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.plot.pie.html#pandas.Series.plot.pie).
If your data includes any `NaN`, they will be automatically filled with 0.
A `ValueError` will be raised if there are any negative values in your data.

```
In [85]: series = pd.Series(3 * np.random.rand(4), index=["a", "b", "c", "d"], name="series")
In [86]: series.plot.pie(figsize=(6, 6));
```
For pie plots it’s best to use square figures, i.e. a figure aspect ratio 1.
You can create the figure with equal width and height, or force the aspect ratio
to be equal after plotting by calling `ax.set_aspect('equal')` on the returned
`axes` object.

Note that pie plot with [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) requires that you either specify a
target column by the `y` argument or `subplots=True`. When `y` is
specified, pie plot of selected column will be drawn. If `subplots=True` is
specified, pie plots for each column are drawn as subplots. A legend will be
drawn in each pie plots by default; specify `legend=False` to hide it.

```
In [87]: df = pd.DataFrame(
   ....:     3 * np.random.rand(4, 2), index=["a", "b", "c", "d"], columns=["x", "y"]
   ....: )
   ....: 
In [88]: df.plot.pie(subplots=True, figsize=(8, 4));
```
You can use the `labels` and `colors` keywords to specify the labels and colors of each wedge.

Warning

Most pandas plots use the `label` and `color` arguments (note the lack of “s” on those).

payload.breadcrumb: Chart visualization — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Chart visualization[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#chart-visualization) > Pie plot[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#pie-plot)
payload.content:
In [88]: df.plot.pie(subplots=True, figsize=(8, 4));
```
You can use the `labels` and `colors` keywords to specify the labels and colors of each wedge.

Warning

Most pandas plots use the `label` and `color` arguments (note the lack of “s” on those).
To be consistent with [`matplotlib.pyplot.pie()`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.pie.html#matplotlib.pyplot.pie) you must use `labels` and `colors`.

If you want to hide wedge labels, specify `labels=None`.
If `fontsize` is specified, the value will be applied to wedge labels.
Also, other keywords supported by [`matplotlib.pyplot.pie()`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.pie.html#matplotlib.pyplot.pie) can be used.

```
In [89]: series.plot.pie(
   ....:     labels=["AA", "BB", "CC", "DD"],
   ....:     colors=["r", "g", "b", "c"],
   ....:     autopct="%.2f",
   ....:     fontsize=20,
   ....:     figsize=(6, 6),
   ....: );
   ....: 
```
If you pass values whose sum total is less than 1.0 they will be rescaled so that they sum to 1.

```
In [90]: series = pd.Series([0.1] * 4, index=["a", "b", "c", "d"], name="series2")
In [91]: series.plot.pie(figsize=(6, 6));
```
See the [matplotlib pie documentation](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.pie.html) for more.

payload.content:
## Plotting with missing data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#plotting-with-missing-data)

pandas tries to be pragmatic about plotting `DataFrames` or `Series`
that contain missing data. Missing values are dropped, left out, or filled
depending on the plot type.

| Plot Type | NaN Handling | 
|---|---|
| Line | Leave gaps at NaNs | 
| Line (stacked) | Fill 0’s | 
| Bar | Fill 0’s | 
| Scatter | Drop NaNs | 
| Histogram | Drop NaNs (column-wise) | 
| Box | Drop NaNs (column-wise) | 
| Area | Fill 0’s | 
| KDE | Drop NaNs (column-wise) | 
| Hexbin | Drop NaNs | 
| Pie | Fill 0’s | 

If any of these defaults are not what you want, or if you want to be
explicit about how missing values are handled, consider using
[`fillna()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.fillna.html#pandas.DataFrame.fillna) or [`dropna()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.dropna.html#pandas.DataFrame.dropna)
before plotting.

payload.content:
## Andrews curves[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#andrews-curves)

Andrews curves allow one to plot multivariate data as a large number
of curves that are created using the attributes of samples as coefficients
for Fourier series, see the [Wikipedia entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrews_plot)
for more information. By coloring these curves differently for each class
it is possible to visualize data clustering. Curves belonging to samples
of the same class will usually be closer together and form larger structures.

**Note**: The “Iris” dataset is available [here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pandas-dev/pandas/main/pandas/tests/io/data/csv/iris.csv).

```
In [97]: from pandas.plotting import andrews_curves
In [98]: data = pd.read_csv("data/iris.data")
In [99]: plt.figure();
In [100]: andrews_curves(data, "Name");
```
